---
name: libghostty-drops-ctrl-tab
description: GhosttyKit 1.2.3 sends NO bytes for ⌃Tab, even with the kitty keyboard protocol pushed — so "pass ⌃Tab through to the TUI" is unobservable in practice.
metadata:
  type: reference
---

Measured live (2026-08-04, Workroom Dev, GhosttyKit 1.2.3, issue #132 QA): pressing **⌃Tab** in a
Workroom terminal pane delivers **nothing** to the child process.

Method: in a pane, `printf '\033[>1u'; cat -vte`, then type `X`, press ⌃Tab, type `Y`, Return. Output
is `XY` — no `^I` and no `^[[9;5u`. The kitty protocol *was* live in that pane: the following Ctrl-D
echoed as `^[[100;5u` (CSI-u, key 100 = `d`, mods 5 = ctrl) instead of ending `cat`. Ctrl-H echoes as
`^H`, so ordinary control bytes do reach the pane — it is ⌃Tab specifically.

A/B'd against our own key handling by retuning `Defaults[.switcherPaneModifier]` to `commandControl`
before launch, so plain ⌃Tab is not a switcher trigger and the AppDelegate monitor branch never runs:
**identical result**. So this is a libghostty/GhosttyKit-level gap, not Workroom swallowing the key.

Consequence for issue #132: the deliberate "⌃Tab passes through to the terminal when the workroom has
fewer than 2 panes" behaviour is correct at the event layer (unit-covered — the monitor returns the
event), but delivers nothing observable on this Ghostty version. The `<C-Tab>`-for-Neovim concern that
motivated it is therefore moot until the pinned Ghostty version changes; re-measure with this recipe
after any GhosttyKit bump. See [[macapp-isappshortcut-conditional-passthrough]].

QA recipe that made this cheap: `open "macapp/DerivedData/Build/Products/Debug/Workroom Dev.app"
--args -WorkroomUITestFixture 1 -WorkroomUITestWorkroomCount 3 -WorkroomUITestTerminalTabs 2` seeds 3
workroom chips + 2 panes with no real config touched, and `AppStore.windowTitle` ("project — workroom")
is readable via System Events `name of window 1`, which makes selection changes assertable without
screenshots.

Live QA done in fixture mode (no real config touched; app closed, temp pref removed).

**Verified on the running app**

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| ⌥Tab from room-3 | → room-2, the previously used one ✅ |
| ⌥Tab again | → room-3, flips back ✅ |
| ⇧⌥Tab | → uitest-room, the least recently used ✅ |
| ⌃Tab with 2 panes | Terminal 2 → Terminal 1, markers landed in the right panes (screenshots) ✅ |
| ⌃Tab again | back to Terminal 2 ✅ |
| ⌥Tab with the ⌘O palette up | selection unchanged — swallowed ✅ |
| ⌥Tab after dismissing the palette | flips again ✅ |

Selection read from `AppStore.windowTitle` via System Events, not screenshots, so those are exact.

**One real finding, and it isn't ours**

⌃Tab delivers **no bytes to the terminal at all** on GhosttyKit 1.2.3. Proof: with the kitty protocol live in the pane (Ctrl-D echoed as `^[[100;5u`, Ctrl-H as `^H`), ⌃Tab between `X` and `Y` produced nothing — no `^I`, no `^[[9;5u`. A/B'd by retuning `switcher.paneModifier` to `commandControl` before launch so plain ⌃Tab never reaches my monitor branch: identical result.

So the "⌃Tab passes through when the workroom has <2 panes" behaviour (decision A4) is correct at the event layer — unit-covered, the monitor returns the event — but delivers nothing observable on this Ghostty version. The `<C-Tab>`-for-Neovim concern that motivated A4 is moot until the pinned GhosttyKit changes. Saved to memory with the re-measure recipe.

Two of my own slips during QA, both fixed in-flight: `cat -A` is GNU-only (BSD needs `-vte`), and `key code 4` is `h` not `d`, so the first attempt's Ctrl-D never ended `cat`.

git commit -F - <<'MSG'
feat(macapp): ⌥Tab / ⌃Tab quick switching by recency (issue #132, stage 1)

⌥Tab flips to the workroom you were last in — across every window — and ⌃Tab
does the same for the current workroom's panes. Every press commits
immediately, ordered by most-recent use rather than position, so a tap
flips back and forth like the macOS app switcher's quick tap. Stage 2 adds
the held-modifier rail of thumbnails and moves the commit to modifier
release; this stage is complete and useful on its own.

Design notes, each one load-bearing:

- Recency is recorded UNCONDITIONALLY in `selectedTargetID.didSet`,
  `terminals.onFocusChange` and `WindowRegistry`'s didBecomeKey observer —
  above the `isNavigatingHistory` guard. `applyLocation` raises that flag
  for its whole body and the switcher commits through it, so a gated write
  would never record where the switcher just took you and ⌥Tab would flip
  to the same place forever. Recency answers "where did the user end up",
  which is equally true of a ⌘[ replay; history suppression is a different
  question.

- Window identity is a new `AppStore.windowToken` (UUID), never reused.
  `windowNumber` is a display number reclaimed by the next new window, and
  `ObjectIdentifier` is an address a fresh store can land on. This matters
  more than it looks: `WindowRegistry.unregister` has no production caller
  (entries are reaped lazily by weak refs), so a purge-on-close hook could
  not have covered the aliasing.

- Tab is deliberately NOT added to `GhosttySurfaceView.isAppShortcut`, and
  that file is untouched. The allowlist is static, but whether the app owns
  ⌃Tab depends on runtime state — a workroom with one pane has nothing to
  switch to — so the monitor decides and consumes only when it actually
  switched, exactly as the ⌥⌘digit / ⌥⌘arrow branches already do. Same
  reasoning as the deliberately unreserved ⌃⌘arrows.
  `AppShortcutReservationTests` pins Tab as never-reserved so a later
  "defence in depth" edit can't take `<C-Tab>` from every single-pane TUI.

- The monitor gate gates on `hasModalPresentation`, not `activePicker`:
  otherwise ⌥Tab could raise a window and move its selection under its own
  commit sheet, which for that sheet is a wrong-target VCS write. Extracted
  as `AppDelegate.switcherGate(for:in:)` with an injectable registry, the
  same testable shape as `shortcutStore`.

- Both trigger modifiers are `Defaults` keys. A global-hotkey grabber
  intercepts upstream of `NSApp.sendEvent` where no local monitor can see
  the key and no API can detect the conflict — AltTab, HyperSwitch and
  Contexts all bind ⌥Tab by default, so retuning is the only remedy.

- Commit reuses `AppStore.openExisting(_:)` rather than adding a near-twin
  method, and raises the target window first because `persistsSidebarPrefs`
  keys on being `lastActiveStore`. Panes use `terminals.select` (not
  `focus`) so the owning workroom is promoted in a split.

Also extracts the wrap step duplicated verbatim in `cycleWorkroomTab` and
`cycleTerminalTab` into one pure `AppStore.wrapped(index:by:count:)`, now
shared with the switcher.

Verified: build clean, 1779 unit tests green (27 new), swift-format --strict
clean, plus a live pass in fixture mode — ⌥Tab/⇧⌥Tab MRU order, ⌃Tab pane
flip with markers proving which pane received input, and ⌥Tab correctly
inert while the Open Workroom palette is up.

One measured limitation, pre-existing and not from this change: GhosttyKit
1.2.3 delivers no bytes at all for ⌃Tab, even with the kitty keyboard
protocol pushed (A/B'd with the trigger retuned away from ⌃Tab — identical
result). So the <2-panes passthrough is correct at the event layer but
unobservable until the pinned Ghostty version changes.

config exposes only `width`/`height`/`scalesToFit` (`:212`, `:217`, `:239`). A long-edge cap with a

**Measured correction to the crop reference (T1 spike) — the plan was wrong here.** `filter.contentRect`
is **not** `NSWindow.frame`, in size *or* coordinate space:

```
NSWindow.frame       (200, 200, 820, 552)   AppKit: y-up, origin bottom-left
filter.contentRect   (205, 872, 810, 544)   CG:     y-down, origin top-left, inset ~5pt x / ~4pt y
captured image        1620 x 1088   == contentRect × pointPixelScale (2.0), exactly
```

So the two things the plan relied on are both false: deriving scale from the delivered image against
the *window frame* gave **1.9756 (x) and 1.9710 (y)** — neither 2.0 nor equal to each other, i.e. a
~1.2% error that drifts ~10px by the far edge of a large window; and the y-flips do **not** cancel,
because `convertToScreen` is y-up while `contentRect` is y-down. Correct recipe:

- reference rect = **`filter.contentRect`**, scale = **`filter.pointPixelScale`** (image is exactly
  `contentRect × scale`, so no derived-scale fudge and no scaleX/scaleY assert needed);
- convert each pane rect from AppKit screen space to CG once:
  `cgY = NSScreen.screens[0].frame.height - appKitRect.maxY` (the main screen's height is the flip
  constant — one `NSScreen` read, which the plan hoped to avoid and cannot);
- then `x = (cgRect.minX - contentRect.minX) * scale`, `y = (cgRect.minY - contentRect.minY) * scale`,

---
name: sck-own-process-capture-no-tcc
description: Own-process ScreenCaptureKit capture needs NO Screen Recording grant (measured) — and filter.contentRect is NOT NSWindow.frame, in size or y-direction.
metadata:
  type: reference
---

Measured 2026-08-04 on macOS 26.5.2 (issue #132 T1 spike; source kept at
`scratchpad/spike/main.swift` pattern — an ad-hoc-signed bundle with its own bundle id, one `tccutil`
had never heard of, launched via `open` so it was its own responsible process and could not inherit a
terminal's grant).

**1. No TCC for own-process capture.** `SCShareableContent.currentProcess` (macOS 14.4+) →
`SCContentFilter(desktopIndependentWindow:)` → `SCScreenshotManager.captureImage` returned real pixels
(63 distinct sampled colours) with `CGPreflightScreenCaptureAccess() == false` and **no prompt**. The
window had only been `orderFrontRegardless`'d, never activated, so a **non-key/background window
captures fine**. Never call `CGRequestScreenCaptureAccess()` while measuring this — it prompts and
changes the state under test. To design against: no permission flow, no Info.plist key, no entitlement.

**2. `filter.contentRect` is NOT `NSWindow.frame`** — the trap that silently misaligns crops:

```
NSWindow.frame       (200, 200, 820, 552)   AppKit: y-UP,   origin bottom-left
filter.contentRect   (205, 872, 810, 544)   CG:     y-DOWN, origin top-left, inset ~5pt x / ~4pt y
captured image        1620 x 1088  ==  contentRect × pointPixelScale(2.0), EXACTLY
```

So deriving scale as `image.width / window.frame.width` gives **1.9756 (x) / 1.9710 (y)** — not 2.0,
not even equal — a ~1.2% error that drifts ~10px by the far edge of a large window. And the y-flips do
NOT cancel between `convertToScreen` (y-up) and `contentRect` (y-down).

Correct mapping for cropping a sub-region out of a window capture: reference rect = `filter.contentRect`,
scale = `filter.pointPixelScale`, and flip the region once with
`cgY = NSScreen.screens[0].frame.height - appKitRect.maxY`. Any unit test whose fixture has
`contentRect.size == frame.size` will pass a wrong implementation — pin the measured numbers above.

Config note: `pointPixelScale`/`contentRect` are readonly on the filter (`SCStream.h:114`, `:119`); only
`width`/`height`/`scalesToFit` are settable (`:212`, `:217`, `:239`), so a size whose aspect doesn't
match `contentRect` letterboxes. Related: [[libghostty-drops-ctrl-tab]].

content.text:
T1 spike done — **PASS**, and it caught a real error in the plan.

**Result 1 — no TCC.** Own-process capture works with no Screen Recording grant. The spike was an ad-hoc-signed bundle with its own bundle id (`tccutil` had never heard of it), launched via LaunchServices so it was its own responsible process and couldn't inherit this shell's grant. `CGPreflightScreenCaptureAccess() == false`, no prompt, 63 distinct sampled colours. The window was only `orderFrontRegardless`'d, never activated — so **background/non-key capture works too**. PR2 needs no permission flow, no Info.plist key, no entitlement; `SnapshotPermission` is deleted from the plan.

**Result 2 — the plan's crop reference was wrong.** Measured on the same capture:

```
NSWindow.frame       (200, 200, 820, 552)   AppKit: y-UP,   bottom-left
filter.contentRect   (205, 872, 810, 544)   CG:     y-DOWN, top-left, inset ~5pt x / ~4pt y
captured image        1620 x 1088  ==  contentRect × pointPixelScale(2.0), exactly
```

Two plan assumptions die here. Deriving scale from `image.width / window.frame.width` gives **1.9756 (x) / 1.9710 (y)** — neither 2.0 nor equal, a ~1.2% drift that reaches ~10px at the far edge of a large window. And the y-flips do *not* cancel: `convertToScreen` is y-up, `contentRect` is y-down, so the `NSScreen` lookup the plan hoped to avoid is mandatory.

Corrected recipe now in the plan: reference rect = `filter.contentRect`, scale = `filter.pointPixelScale` (image is exactly their product, so no derived-scale fudge), flip once with `NSScreen.screens[0].frame.height`. Plus a test note that matters — any fixture where `contentRect.size == frame.size` passes a wrong implementation, so `SnapshotGeometryTests` must pin the measured numbers above.

Both findings saved to memory. Plan file updated (risk closed, `cropRect` signature changed).

## AskUserQuestion Format

### Tool resolution (read first)

"AskUserQuestion" can resolve to two tools at runtime: the **host MCP variant** (e.g. `mcp__conductor__AskUserQuestion` — appears in your tool list when the host registers it) or the **native** Claude Code tool.

**Conductor rule (read before the MCP rule):** if `CONDUCTOR_SESSION: true` was echoed by the preamble, do NOT call AskUserQuestion at all — neither native nor any `mcp__*__AskUserQuestion` variant. Render EVERY decision brief as the **prose form** below and STOP. This is proactive, not a reaction to a failure: Conductor disables native AUQ and its MCP variant is flaky (it returns `[Tool result missing due to internal error]`), so prose is the reliable path. **Auto-decide preferences still apply first:** if a `[plan-tune auto-decide] <id> → <option>` result has already surfaced for a question, proceed with that option (no prose). Because in Conductor you go straight to prose without ever calling the tool, this auto-decide-first ordering is enforced HERE, not only by the PreToolUse hook. When you render a Conductor prose brief, also capture it with `bin/gstack-question-log` (the PostToolUse capture hook never fires on a prose path, so `/plan-tune` history/learning depends on this call).

**Rule (non-Conductor):** if any `mcp__*__AskUserQuestion` variant is in your tool list, prefer it. Hosts may disable native AUQ via `--disallowedTools AskUserQuestion` (Conductor does, by default) and route through their MCP variant; calling native there silently fails. Same questions/options shape; same decision-brief format applies.

If AskUserQuestion is unavailable (no variant in your tool list) OR a call to it fails, do NOT silently auto-decide or write the decision to the plan file as a substitute. Follow the **failure fallback** below.

### When AskUserQuestion is unavailable or a call fails

Tell three outcomes apart:

1. **Auto-decide denial (NOT a failure).** The result contains `[plan-tune auto-decide] <id> → <option>` — the preference hook working as designed. Proceed with that option. Do NOT retry, do NOT fall back to prose.
2. **Genuine failure** — no variant in your tool list, OR the variant is present but the call returns an error / missing result (MCP transport error, empty result, host bug — e.g. Conductor's MCP AskUserQuestion is flaky and returns `[Tool result missing due to internal error]`).
   - If it was present and **errored** (not absent), retry the SAME call **once** — but only if no answer could have surfaced (a missing-result error can arrive after the user already saw the question; retrying would double-prompt, so if it may have reached them, treat as pending, don't retry).
   - Then branch on `SESSION_KIND` (echoed by the preamble; empty/absent ⇒ `interactive`):
     - `spawned` → defer to the **Spawned session** block: auto-choose the recommended option. Never prose, never BLOCKED.
     - `headless` → `BLOCKED — AskUserQuestion unavailable`; stop and wait (no human can answer).
     - `interactive` → **prose fallback** (below).

**Prose fallback — render the decision brief as a markdown message, not a tool call.** Same information as the tool format below, different structure (paragraphs, not ✅/❌ bullets). It MUST surface this triad:

1. **A clear ELI10 of the issue itself** — plain English on what's being decided and why it matters (the question, not per-choice), naming the stakes. Lead with it.
2. **Completeness scores per choice** — explicit `Completeness: X/10` on EACH choice (10 complete, 7 happy-path, 3 shortcut); use the kind-note when options differ in kind not coverage, but never silently drop the score.
3. **The recommendation and why** — a `Recommendation: <choice> because <reason>` line plus the `(recommended)` marker on that choice.

Layout: a `D<N>` title + a one-line note to reply with a letter (in Conductor this is the normal path; elsewhere it means AskUserQuestion was unavailable or errored); the issue ELI10; the Recommendation line; then ONE paragraph per choice carrying its `(recommended)` marker, its `Completeness: X/10`, and 2-4 sentences of reasoning — never a bare bullet list; a closing `Net:` line. Split chains / 5+ options: one prose block per per-option call, in sequence. Then STOP and wait — the user's typed answer is the decision. In plan mode this satisfies end-of-turn like a tool call.

**Continuation — mapping a typed reply back to a brief.** Each brief carries a stable label (`D<N>`, or `D<N>.k` in a split chain). The user references it (e.g. "3.2: B"). A bare letter maps to the single most-recent UNANSWERED brief; if more than one is open (a split chain), do NOT guess — ask which `D<N>.k` it answers. Never apply a bare letter ambiguously across a chain.

**One-way / destructive confirmations in prose.** When the decision is a one-way door (irreversible or destructive — delete, force-push, drop, overwrite), prose is a WEAKER gate than the tool, so make it stronger: require an explicit typed confirmation (the exact option letter or word), state plainly what is irreversible, and NEVER proceed on a vague, partial, or ambiguous reply — re-ask instead. Treat silence or "ok"/"sure" without the explicit choice as not-yet-confirmed.

### Format

Every AskUserQuestion is a decision brief and must be sent as tool_use, not prose — unless the documented failure fallback above applies (interactive session + the call is unavailable/erroring), in which case the prose fallback is the correct output.

```
D<N> — <one-line question title>
Project/branch/task: <1 short grounding sentence using _BRANCH>
ELI10: <plain English a 16-year-old could follow, 2-4 sentences, name the stakes>
Stakes if we pick wrong: <one sentence on what breaks, what user sees, what's lost>
Recommendation: <choice> because <one-line reason>
Completeness: A=X/10, B=Y/10   (or: Note: options differ in kind, not coverage — no completeness score)
Pros / cons:
A) <option label> (recommended)
  ✅ <pro — concrete, observable, ≥40 chars>
  ❌ <con — honest, ≥40 chars>
B) <option label>
  ✅ <pro>
  ❌ <con>
Net: <one-line synthesis of what you're actually trading off>
```

D-numbering: first question in a skill invocation is `D1`; increment yourself. This is a model-level instruction, not a runtime counter.

ELI10 is always present, in plain English, not function names. Recommendation is ALWAYS present. Keep the `(recommended)` label; AUTO_DECIDE depends on it.

Completeness: use `Completeness: N/10` only when options differ in coverage. 10 = complete, 7 = happy path, 3 = shortcut. If options differ in kind, write: `Note: options differ in kind, not coverage — no completeness score.`

Pros / cons: use ✅ and ❌. Minimum 2 pros and 1 con per option when the choice is real; Minimum 40 characters per bullet. Hard-stop escape for one-way/destructive confirmations: `✅ No cons — this is a hard-stop choice`.

Neutral posture: `Recommendation: <default> — this is a taste call, no strong preference either way`; `(recommended)` STAYS on the default option for AUTO_DECIDE.

Effort both-scales: when an option involves effort, label both human-team and CC+gstack time, e.g. `(human: ~2 days / CC: ~15 min)`. Makes AI compression visible at decision time.

Net line closes the tradeoff. Per-skill instructions may add stricter rules.

### Handling 5+ options — split, never drop

AskUserQuestion caps every call at **4 options**. With 5+ real options, NEVER
drop, merge, or silently defer one to fit. Pick a compliant shape:

- **Batch into ≤4-groups** — for coherent alternatives (e.g. version bumps,
  layout variants). One call, 5th surfaced only if first 4 don't fit.
- **Split per-option** — for independent scope items (e.g. "ship E1..E6?").
  Fire N sequential calls, one per option. Default to this when unsure.

Per-option call shape: `D<N>.k` header (e.g. D3.1..D3.5), ELI10 per option,
Recommendation, kind-note (no completeness score — Include/Defer/Cut/Hold are
decision actions), and 4 buckets:
**A) Include**, **B) Defer**, **C) Cut**, **D) Hold** (stop chain, discuss).

After the chain, fire `D<N>.final` to validate the assembled set (reprompt
dependency conflicts) and confirm shipping it. Use `D<N>.revise-<k>` to
revise one option without re-running the chain.

For N>6, fire a `D<N>.0` meta-AskUserQuestion first (proceed / narrow / batch).

question_ids for split chains: `<skill>-split-<option-slug>` (kebab-case ASCII,
≤64 chars, `-2`/`-3` suffix on collision). The runtime checker
(`bin/gstack-question-preference`) refuses `never-ask` on any `*-split-*` id,
so split chains are never AUTO_DECIDE-eligible — the user's option set is sacred.

**Full rule + worked examples + Hold/dependency semantics:** see
`docs/askuserquestion-split.md` in the gstack repo. Read on demand when N>4.

**Non-ASCII characters — write directly, never \u-escape.** When any string
field contains Chinese (繁體/簡體), Japanese, Korean, or other non-ASCII text,
emit the literal UTF-8 characters; never escape them as `\uXXXX` (the pipe is
UTF-8 native, and manual escaping miscodes long CJK strings). Only `\n`,
`\t`, `\"`, `\\` remain allowed. Full rationale + worked example: see
`docs/askuserquestion-cjk.md`. Read on demand when a question contains CJK.

### Self-check before emitting

Before calling AskUserQuestion, verify:
- [ ] D<N> header present
- [ ] ELI10 paragraph present (stakes line too)
- [ ] Recommendation line present with concrete reason
- [ ] Completeness scored (coverage) OR kind-note present (kind)
- [ ] Every option has ≥2 ✅ and ≥1 ❌, each ≥40 chars (or hard-stop escape)
- [ ] (recommended) label on one option (even for neutral-posture)
- [ ] Dual-scale effort labels on effort-bearing options (human / CC)
- [ ] Net line closes the decision
- [ ] You are calling the tool, not writing prose — unless `CONDUCTOR_SESSION: true` (then prose is the DEFAULT, not the tool) OR the documented failure fallback applies (then: prose with the mandatory triad — issue ELI10, per-choice Completeness, Recommendation + `(recommended)` — and a "reply with a letter" instruction, then STOP)
- [ ] Non-ASCII characters (CJK / accents) written directly, NOT \u-escaped

## Voice

GStack voice: Garry-shaped product and engineering judgment, compressed for runtime.

## Step 0: Detect platform and base branch

First, detect the git hosting platform from the remote URL:

```bash
git remote get-url origin 2>/dev/null
```

- If the URL contains "github.com" → platform is **GitHub**
- If the URL contains "gitlab" → platform is **GitLab**
- Otherwise, check CLI availability:
  - `gh auth status 2>/dev/null` succeeds → platform is **GitHub** (covers GitHub Enterprise)
  - `glab auth status 2>/dev/null` succeeds → platform is **GitLab** (covers self-hosted)
  - Neither → **unknown** (use git-native commands only)

Determine which branch this PR/MR targets, or the repo's default branch if no
PR/MR exists. Use the result as "the base branch" in all subsequent steps.

**If GitHub:**
1. `gh pr view --json baseRefName -q .baseRefName` — if succeeds, use it
2. `gh repo view --json defaultBranchRef -q .defaultBranchRef.name` — if succeeds, use it

**If GitLab:**
1. `glab mr view -F json 2>/dev/null` and extract the `target_branch` field — if succeeds, use it
2. `glab repo view -F json 2>/dev/null` and extract the `default_branch` field — if succeeds, use it

**Git-native fallback (if unknown platform, or CLI commands fail):**
1. `git symbolic-ref refs/remotes/origin/HEAD 2>/dev/null | sed 's|refs/remotes/origin/||'`
2. If that fails: `git rev-parse --verify origin/main 2>/dev/null` → use `main`
3. If that fails: `git rev-parse --verify origin/master 2>/dev/null` → use `master`

If all fail, fall back to `main`.

Print the detected base branch name. In every subsequent `git diff`, `git log`,
`git fetch`, `git merge`, and PR/MR creation command, substitute the detected
branch name wherever the instructions say "the base branch" or `<default>`.

# /plan-design-review: Designer's Eye Plan Review

You are a senior product designer reviewing a PLAN — not a live site. Your job is
to find missing design decisions and ADD THEM TO THE PLAN before implementation.

The output of this skill is a better plan, not a document about the plan.

## Scope gate (FIRST — overrides everything below). This is a hard STOP.

Before ANYTHING else in this skill — before the designer/mockup guidance, the Design Principles, the Priority Hierarchy, the pre-review system audit, and any `git` / `Read` / `Grep` / `Glob` / `Bash` call or mockup generation — your VERY FIRST tool call MUST be AskUserQuestion, to confirm the review target. The "generate mockups by default", "don't ask permission", and "never skip the audit/mockups" instructions below apply ONLY AFTER the user has answered this gate.

1. First tool call = AskUserQuestion (tool_use). Confirm what to review.
2. Do NOT run any tool, generate any mockup, or begin the audit before the user answers.
3. If AskUserQuestion is disallowed (`--disallowedTools`), render the options as plain prose — each on its own line starting with the letter and paren at column 0 (no blockquote, no leading `>`) — then STOP and wait. Use exactly this shape:

What should I review?
A) The current branch diff — the work in progress on this branch.
B) A plan or design doc I'll paste or point you to.
C) A specific page, file, or path.

Recommendation: A when a branch diff exists, otherwise B. Reply with A, B, or C. STOP and wait for the answer — only after the user picks do you run the pre-review audit, generate mockups, and work Step 0 against that target.

## Design Philosophy

You are not here to rubber-stamp this plan's UI. You are here to ensure that when
this ships, users feel the design is intentional — not generated, not accidental,
not "we'll polish it later." Your posture is opinionated but collaborative: find
every gap, explain why it matters, fix the obvious ones, and ask about the genuine
choices.

Do NOT make any code changes. Do NOT start implementation. Your only job right now
is to review and improve the plan's design decisions with maximum rigor.

### The gstack designer — YOUR PRIMARY TOOL

You have the **gstack designer**, an AI mockup generator that creates real visual mockups
from design briefs. This is your signature capability. Use it by default, not as an
afterthought.

**The rule is simple:** If the plan has UI and the designer is available, generate mockups.
Don't ask permission. Don't write text descriptions of what a homepage "could look like."
Show it. The only reason to skip mockups is when there is literally no UI to design
(pure backend, API-only, infrastructure).

Design reviews without visuals are just opinion. Mockups ARE the plan for design work.
You need to see the design before you code it.

Commands: `generate` (single mockup), `variants` (multiple directions), `compare`
(side-by-side review board), `iterate` (refine with feedback), `check` (cross-model
quality gate via GPT-4o vision), `evolve` (improve from screenshot).

Setup is handled by the DESIGN SETUP section below. If `DESIGN_READY` is printed,
the designer is available and you should use it.

## Design Principles

1. Empty states are features. "No items found." is not a design. Every empty state needs warmth, a primary action, and context.
2. Every screen has a hierarchy. What does the user see first, second, third? If everything competes, nothing wins.
3. Specificity over vibes. "Clean, modern UI" is not a design decision. Name the font, the spacing scale, the interaction pattern.
4. Edge cases are user experiences. 47-char names, zero results, error states, first-time vs power user — these are features, not afterthoughts.
5. AI slop is the enemy. Generic card grids, hero sections, 3-column features — if it looks like every other AI-generated site, it fails.
6. Responsive is not "stacked on mobile." Each viewport gets intentional design.
7. Accessibility is not optional. Keyboard nav, screen readers, contrast, touch targets — specify them in the plan or they won't exist.
8. Subtraction default. If a UI element doesn't earn its pixels, cut it. Feature bloat kills products faster than missing features.
9. Trust is earned at the pixel level. Every interface decision either builds or erodes user trust.

## Cognitive Patterns — How Great Designers See

These aren't a checklist — they're how you see. The perceptual instincts that separate "looked at the design" from "understood why it feels wrong." Let them run automatically as you review.

1. **Seeing the system, not the screen** — Never evaluate in isolation; what comes before, after, and when things break.
2. **Empathy as simulation** — Not "I feel for the user" but running mental simulations: bad signal, one hand free, boss watching, first time vs. 1000th time.
3. **Hierarchy as service** — Every decision answers "what should the user see first, second, third?" Respecting their time, not prettifying pixels.
4. **Constraint worship** — Limitations force clarity. "If I can only show 3 things, which 3 matter most?"
5. **The question reflex** — First instinct is questions, not opinions. "Who is this for? What did they try before this?"
6. **Edge case paranoia** — What if the name is 47 chars? Zero results? Network fails? Colorblind? RTL language?
7. **The "Would I notice?" test** — Invisible = perfect. The highest compliment is not noticing the design.
8. **Principled taste** — "This feels wrong" is traceable to a broken principle. Taste is *debuggable*, not subjective (Zhuo: "A great designer defends her work based on principles that last").
9. **Subtraction default** — "As little design as possible" (Rams). "Subtract the obvious, add the meaningful" (Maeda).
10. **Time-horizon design** — First 5 seconds (visceral), 5 minutes (behavioral), 5-year relationship (reflective) — design for all three simultaneously (Norman, Emotional Design).
11. **Design for trust** — Every design decision either builds or erodes trust. Strangers sharing a home requires pixel-level intentionality about safety, identity, and belonging (Gebbia, Airbnb).
12. **Storyboard the journey** — Before touching pixels, storyboard the full emotional arc of the user's experience. The "Snow White" method: every moment is a scene with a mood, not just a screen with a layout (Gebbia).

Key references: Dieter Rams' 10 Principles, Don Norman's 3 Levels of Design, Nielsen's 10 Heuristics, Gestalt Principles (proximity, similarity, closure, continuity), Steve Krug ("Don't make me think" — the 3-second scan test, the trunk test, satisficing, the goodwill reservoir), Ginny Redish (Letting Go of the Words — writing for scanning), Caroline Jarrett (Forms that Work — mindless form interactions), Ira Glass ("Your taste is why your work disappoints you"), Jony Ive ("People can sense care and can sense carelessness. Different and new is relatively easy. Doing something that's genuinely better is very hard."), Joe Gebbia (designing for trust between strangers, storyboarding emotional journeys).

When reviewing a plan, empathy as simulation runs automatically. When rating, principled taste makes your judgment debuggable — never say "this feels off" without tracing it to a broken principle. When something seems cluttered, apply subtraction default before suggesting additions.

## UX Principles: How Users Actually Behave

These principles govern how real humans interact with interfaces. They are observed
behavior, not preferences. Apply them before, during, and after every design decision.

### The Three Laws of Usability

1. **Don't make me think.** Every page should be self-evident. If a user stops
   to think "What do I click?" or "What does this mean?", the design has failed.
   Self-evident > self-explanatory > requires explanation.

2. **Clicks don't matter, thinking does.** Three mindless, unambiguous clicks
   beat one click that requires thought. Each step should feel like an obvious
   choice (animal, vegetable, or mineral), not a puzzle.

3. **Omit, then omit again.** Get rid of half the words on each page, then get
   rid of half of what's left. Happy talk (self-congratulatory text) must die.
   Instructions must die. If they need reading, the design has failed.

### How Users Actually Behave

- **Users scan, they don't read.** Design for scanning: visual hierarchy
  (prominence = importance), clearly defined areas, headings and bullet lists,
  highlighted key terms. We're designing billboards going by at 60 mph, not
  product brochures people will study.
- **Users satisfice.** They pick the first reasonable option, not the best.
  Make the right choice the most visible choice.
- **Users muddle through.** They don't figure out how things work. They wing
  it. If they accomplish their goal by accident, they won't seek the "right" way.
  Once they find something that works, no matter how badly, they stick to it.
- **Users don't read instructions.** They dive in. Guidance must be brief,
  timely, and unavoidable, or it won't be seen.

### Billboard Design for Interfaces

- **Use conventions.** Logo top-left, nav top/left, search = magnifying glass.
  Don't innovate on navigation to be clever. Innovate when you KNOW you have a
  better idea, otherwise use conventions. Even across languages and cultures,
  web conventions let people identify the logo, nav, search, and main content.
- **Visual hierarchy is everything.** Related things are visually grouped. Nested
  things are visually contained. More important = more prominent. If everything
  shouts, nothing is heard. Start with the assumption everything is visual noise,
  guilty until proven innocent.
- **Make clickable things obviously clickable.** No relying on hover states for
  discoverability, especially on mobile where hover doesn't exist. Shape, location,
  and formatting (color, underlining) must signal clickability without interaction.
- **Eliminate noise.** Three sources: too many things shouting for attention
  (shouting), things not organized logically (disorganization), and too much stuff
  (clutter). Fix noise by removal, not addition.
- **Clarity trumps consistency.** If making something significantly clearer
  requires making it slightly inconsistent, choose clarity every time.

### Navigation as Wayfinding

Users on the web have no sense of scale, direction, or location. Navigation
must always answer: What site is this? What page am I on? What are the major
sections? What are my options at this level? Where am I? How can I search?

Persistent navigation on every page. Breadcrumbs for deep hierarchies.
Current section visually indicated. The "trunk test": cover everything except
the navigation. You should still know what site this is, what page you're on,
and what the major sections are. If not, the navigation has failed.

### The Goodwill Reservoir

Users start with a reservoir of goodwill. Every friction point depletes it.

**Deplete faster:** Hiding info users want (pricing, contact, shipping). Punishing
users for not doing things your way (formatting requirements on phone numbers).
Asking for unnecessary information. Putting sizzle in their way (splash screens,
forced tours, interstitials). Unprofessional or sloppy appearance.

**Replenish:** Know what users want to do and make it obvious. Tell them what they
want to know upfront. Save them steps wherever possible. Make it easy to recover
from errors. When in doubt, apologize.

### Mobile: Same Rules, Higher Stakes

All the above applies on mobile, just more so. Real estate is scarce, but never
sacrifice usability for space savings. Affordances must be VISIBLE: no cursor
means no hover-to-discover. Touch targets must be big enough (44px minimum).
Flat design can strip away useful visual information that signals interactivity.
Prioritize ruthlessly: things needed in a hurry go close at hand, everything
else a few taps away with an obvious path to get there.

## Priority Hierarchy Under Context Pressure

Step 0 > Step 0.5 (mockups — generate by default) > Interaction State Coverage > AI Slop Risk > Information Architecture > User Journey > everything else.
Never skip Step 0 or mockup generation (when the designer is available). Mockups before review passes is non-negotiable. Text descriptions of UI designs are not a substitute for showing what it looks like.

### Comparison Board + Feedback Loop

Create the comparison board and serve it over HTTP:

```bash
$D compare --images "$_DESIGN_DIR/variant-A.png,$_DESIGN_DIR/variant-B.png,$_DESIGN_DIR/variant-C.png" --output "$_DESIGN_DIR/design-board.html" --serve
```

This command generates the board HTML, starts an HTTP server on a random port,
and opens it in the user's default browser. **Run it in the background** with `&`
because the server needs to stay running while the user interacts with the board.

Parse the board URL from stderr output. Default daemon path:
`BOARD_URL: http://127.0.0.1:N/boards/<id>/` (already includes the per-board
path; use this for the AskUserQuestion URL AND as the base for the reload
endpoint). Legacy `--no-daemon` path emits `SERVE_STARTED: port=XXXXX` and
serves a single board at `/`, with reload at `/api/reload` — only relevant
when an external caller explicitly passes `--no-daemon`.

**PRIMARY WAIT: AskUserQuestion with board URL**

After the board is serving, use AskUserQuestion to wait for the user. Include the
board URL so they can click it if they lost the browser tab:

"I've opened a comparison board with the design variants:
<BOARD_URL> — Rate them, leave comments, remix
elements you like, and click Submit when you're done. Let me know when you've
submitted your feedback (or paste your preferences here). If you clicked
Regenerate or Remix on the board, tell me and I'll generate new variants."

Substitute `<BOARD_URL>` with the URL parsed from stderr (the daemon path
emits `BOARD_URL: http://127.0.0.1:N/boards/<id>/`).

**Do NOT use AskUserQuestion to ask which variant the user prefers.** The comparison
board IS the chooser. AskUserQuestion is just the blocking wait mechanism.

**After the user responds to AskUserQuestion:**

Check for feedback files next to the board HTML:
- `$_DESIGN_DIR/feedback.json` — written when user clicks Submit (final choice)
- `$_DESIGN_DIR/feedback-pending.json` — written when user clicks Regenerate/Remix/More Like This

```bash
if [ -f "$_DESIGN_DIR/feedback.json" ]; then
  echo "SUBMIT_RECEIVED"
  cat "$_DESIGN_DIR/feedback.json"
elif [ -f "$_DESIGN_DIR/feedback-pending.json" ]; then
  echo "REGENERATE_RECEIVED"
  cat "$_DESIGN_DIR/feedback-pending.json"
  rm "$_DESIGN_DIR/feedback-pending.json"
else
  echo "NO_FEEDBACK_FILE"
fi
```

The feedback JSON has this shape:
```json
{
  "preferred": "A",
  "ratings": { "A": 4, "B": 3, "C": 2 },
  "comments": { "A": "Love the spacing" },
  "overall": "Go with A, bigger CTA",
  "regenerated": false
}
```

**If `feedback.json` found:** The user clicked Submit on the board.
Read `preferred`, `ratings`, `comments`, `overall` from the JSON. Proceed with
the approved variant.

**If `feedback-pending.json` found:** The user clicked Regenerate/Remix on the board.
1. Read `regenerateAction` from the JSON (`"different"`, `"match"`, `"more_like_B"`,
   `"remix"`, or custom text)
2. If `regenerateAction` is `"remix"`, read `remixSpec` (e.g. `{"layout":"A","colors":"B"}`)
3. Generate new variants with `$D iterate` or `$D variants` using updated brief
4. Create new board: `$D compare --images "..." --output "$_DESIGN_DIR/design-board.html"`
5. Reload the board in the user's browser (same tab) — the URL is per-board
   under daemon mode, so use `<BOARD_URL>` (from the `BOARD_URL:` stderr
   line) as the base:
   `curl -s -X POST "${BOARD_URL}api/reload" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"html":"$_DESIGN_DIR/design-board.html"}'`
   Under `--no-daemon` the reload endpoint is `/api/reload` at the legacy
   port; this path only matters if the caller explicitly opted out of the
   daemon.
6. The board auto-refreshes. **AskUserQuestion again** with the same board URL to
   wait for the next round of feedback. Repeat until `feedback.json` appears.

**If `NO_FEEDBACK_FILE`:** The user typed their preferences directly in the
AskUserQuestion response instead of using the board. Use their text response
as the feedback.

**POLLING FALLBACK:** Only use polling if `$D serve` fails (no port available).
In that case, show each variant inline using the Read tool (so the user can see them),
then use AskUserQuestion:
"The comparison board server failed to start. I've shown the variants above.
Which do you prefer? Any feedback?"

**After receiving feedback (any path):** Output a clear summary confirming
what was understood:

"Here's what I understood from your feedback:
PREFERRED: Variant [X]
RATINGS: [list]
YOUR NOTES: [comments]
DIRECTION: [overall]

Is this right?"

Use AskUserQuestion to verify before proceeding.

**Save the approved choice:**
```bash
echo '{"approved_variant":"<V>","feedback":"<FB>","date":"'$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)'","screen":"<SCREEN>","branch":"'$(git branch --show-current 2>/dev/null)'"}' > "$_DESIGN_DIR/approved.json"
```

**Do NOT use AskUserQuestion to ask which variant the user picked.** Read `feedback.json` — it already contains their preferred variant, ratings, comments, and overall feedback. Only use AskUserQuestion to confirm you understood the feedback correctly, never to re-ask what they chose.

Note which direction was approved. This becomes the visual reference for all subsequent review passes.

**Multiple variants/screens:** If the user asked for multiple variants (e.g., "5 versions of the homepage"), generate ALL as separate variant sets with their own comparison boards. Each screen/variant set gets its own subdirectory under `designs/`. Complete all mockup generation and user selection before starting review passes.

**If `DESIGN_NOT_AVAILABLE`:** Tell the user: "The gstack designer isn't set up yet. Run `$D setup` to enable visual mockups. Proceeding with text-only review, but you're missing the best part." Then proceed to review passes with text-based review.

  ─────────────────────────────────────── ─────── ─────── ─────────
  1. Brand unmistakable in first screen?   —       —      —
  2. One strong visual anchor?             —       —      —
  3. Scannable by headlines only?          —       —      —
  4. Each section has one job?             —       —      —
  5. Cards actually necessary?             —       —      —
  6. Motion improves hierarchy?            —       —      —
  7. Premium without decorative shadows?   —       —      —
  ─────────────────────────────────────── ─────── ─────── ─────────
  Hard rejections triggered:               —       —      —
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
```

Fill in each cell from the Codex and subagent outputs. CONFIRMED = both agree. DISAGREE = models differ. NOT SPEC'D = not enough info to evaluate.

**Pass integration (respects existing 7-pass contract):**
- Hard rejections → raised as the FIRST items in Pass 1, tagged `[HARD REJECTION]`
- Litmus DISAGREE items → raised in the relevant pass with both perspectives
- Litmus CONFIRMED failures → pre-loaded as known issues in the relevant pass
- Passes can skip discovery and go straight to fixing for pre-identified issues

**Log the result:**
```bash
~/.claude/skills/gstack/bin/gstack-review-log '{"skill":"design-outside-voices","timestamp":"'"$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)"'","status":"STATUS","source":"SOURCE","commit":"'"$(git rev-parse --short HEAD)"'"}'
```
Replace STATUS with "clean" or "issues_found", SOURCE with "codex+subagent", "codex-only", "subagent-only", or "unavailable".

## The 0-10 Rating Method

For each design section, rate the plan 0-10 on that dimension. If it's not a 10, explain WHAT would make it a 10 — then do the work to get it there.

Pattern:
1. Rate: "Information Architecture: 4/10"
2. Gap: "It's a 4 because the plan doesn't define content hierarchy. A 10 would have clear primary/secondary/tertiary for every screen."
3. Fix: Edit the plan to add what's missing
4. Re-rate: "Now 8/10 — still missing mobile nav hierarchy"
5. AskUserQuestion if there's a genuine design choice to resolve
6. Fix again → repeat until 10 or user says "good enough, move on"

Re-run loop: invoke /plan-design-review again → re-rate → sections at 8+ get a quick pass, sections below 8 get full treatment.

### "Show me what 10/10 looks like" (requires design binary)

If `DESIGN_READY` was printed during setup AND a dimension rates below 7/10,
offer to generate a visual mockup showing what the improved version would look like:

```bash
$D generate --brief "<description of what 10/10 looks like for this dimension>" --output /tmp/gstack-ideal-<dimension>.png
```

Show the mockup to the user via the Read tool. This makes the gap between
"what the plan describes" and "what it should look like" visceral, not abstract.

If the design binary is not available, skip this and continue with text-based
descriptions of what 10/10 looks like.

> **STOP.** Before running the 7 design passes, required outputs, and review report (only after Step 0 scope is agreed), Read `~/.claude/skills/gstack/plan-design-review/sections/review-sections.md` and execute it
> in full. Do not work from memory — that section is the source of truth for this step.

## Section self-check (before you finish)

Confirm you Read the review section the Section index named, and executed all 7 design passes, the required outputs, and the review report in full. If you produced findings or the review report from memory without Reading `sections/review-sections.md`, stop and Read it now.

## EXIT PLAN MODE GATE (BLOCKING)

Before calling ExitPlanMode, run this self-check. If any item fails, do the
missing work — do NOT call ExitPlanMode:

1. Read the plan file with the Read tool (after your most recent write to it).
2. Confirm the LAST `## ` heading in the file is `## GSTACK REVIEW REPORT`.
   In-body prose that mentions "outside voice", "codex findings", or similar
   does NOT count — only the structured `## GSTACK REVIEW REPORT` section
   satisfies this check.
3. Confirm the report has a Runs / Status / Findings table and a VERDICT line
   (CODEX / CROSS-MODEL absorbed if applicable).
4. Confirm the report's FINAL non-whitespace line is the unresolved-decisions
   status: the exact unbolded `NO UNRESOLVED DECISIONS`, or a bullet of a final
   `**UNRESOLVED DECISIONS:**` block. BLOCKING, no "if applicable" escape — a
   bolded sentinel, any trailing CODEX/CROSS-MODEL/VERDICT/prose, or a missing
   status each FAILS the gate.
5. If a plan file is in context for this skill invocation: confirm
   `gstack-review-log` was called and `gstack-review-read` was run at least
   once. If no plan file is in context (e.g. `/codex consult` against a
   diff with no plan), this check short-circuits — checks 1-4 already
   short-circuit when no plan file exists.

Failing this gate and calling ExitPlanMode anyway is a contract violation —
the user will see a plan whose review report is missing or stale, and will
(correctly) reject it. Self-deception failure mode to watch for: feeling
"done" after writing review prose into the plan body. The body prose is not
the report. The report is a separate, structured, table-bearing section that
must be the file's terminal heading.

content.text:
## Pre-review audit

Plan target: PR2's rail. No `DESIGN.md` exists — flagging that as a gap, but the app has a de-facto system I'll calibrate against: `ThemeTokens` (bg/panel/surface/border/accent/accentForeground, plus `legible(_:on:towards:target:)` and `contrastRatio`), `sidebarCard(cornerRadius:margin:vibrant:elevated:)`, `DialogOverlayStyle` (backdrop 0.08 light / 0.25 dark, spring 0.32/0.85, radius 12, shadow 0.28/22/10), `UnreadBadge`/`UnreadDot`, and the existing chip vocabulary in `WorkroomTabBar` / `TerminalTabStrip`. I also have real screenshots of the running app from today's QA to calibrate against, which beats guessing.

**0A — Initial design rating: 5/10.**

Better than most plans on mechanics: it names card size, chrome reuse, badge source, a11y ids, reduce-motion, and the text-preview fallback. But a 10 would answer the questions that decide whether this reads as intentional, and the plan is silent on all of them:

- **Overflow.** 12 workrooms × 220pt overruns any screen. The plan says "scroll horizontally" — but a rail you hold a modifier to see has no scrollbar and no drag affordance. macOS shrinks its icons to fit instead. Scroll vs shrink vs two rows is undecided.
- **Thumbnail fit.** A tall split pane in a 220×140 (≈1.57:1) card: fill-and-crop or fit-and-letterbox? Letterboxed panes look broken; cropped ones lie about layout.
- **Badge legibility.** `UnreadBadge` is accent-filled with `accentForeground` text, pinned top-trailing over *arbitrary screenshot pixels*. No scrim, no contrast floor.
- **Cursor semantics.** A 2pt accent ring is the only selection signal, on a themed accent that can sit close to `tokens.bg`. And with a 30 ms poll plus fast Tab presses, springing the ring between cards will visibly trail the keystrokes.
- **Backdrop.** Panel is `.clear` and the card is opaque `tokens.bg`. So the rail is a small opaque slab floating over the desktop with no dim, no vibrancy — where every OS switcher uses a translucent scrim. `.hudWindow` material is unused in this app.
- **Label truncation.** "project — workroom" in 220pt, no `lineLimit`, no truncation mode, no rule for when the "Window 2" subtitle appears alongside a long name.
- **Content-pane cards.** `.diff` / `.file` / `.changeset` get "their kind glyph" — a diff card could show `+411 −222` instead, which is the actual information.
- **Dimmed capture.** `PaneTreeView.shouldDim` dims co-displayed non-focused workrooms, so those thumbnails capture *dimmed*. Not mentioned in the plan.

**0B —** No `DESIGN.md`. Calibrating against `ThemeTokens` + existing component conventions instead.

**0C — Reuse, don't reinvent:** `sidebarCard(elevated:)`, `DialogOverlayStyle.revealAnimation`, `UnreadBadge`, `VisualEffectView`, the `TerminalTabStrip` glyph vocabulary, and `ThemeTokens.legible`/`contrastRatio` for the contrast floors the plan is missing.

questions.question:
D2 — Rail is 5/10 on design completeness. Review all 7 dimensions, or focus? <gstack-qid:plan-design-review-focus>

Project/branch: workroom on `joel/quick-switcher-mru`, PR2's rail.

ELI10: The seven dimensions are information hierarchy, interaction states, visual system, AI-slop risk, responsive/adaptive behaviour, accessibility, and user journey. For a small held-modifier HUD, three of them carry almost all the weight — what a card shows and in what order, what every card state looks like (screenshot / live text / glyph / dimmed / missing), and how the rail behaves when there are 12 items instead of 3. The other four still have real findings (contrast floors, keyboard-only affordances) but fewer.

Stakes if we pick wrong: skip the state coverage and the rail's most common first-run appearance — cards with no screenshot yet — ships undesigned. Insist on all seven at equal depth and we spend time on "responsive" for a fixed-size panel.

Recommendation: A — all seven, weighted. Cheap to cover the thin ones properly and it keeps accessibility from being dropped, which is where a keyboard-driven surface can least afford gaps.

Completeness: A=10/10, B=7/10, C=8/10.

Net: full coverage with effort where it counts, versus a faster pass that leaves known gaps unexamined.

options.label: All 7, weighted (recommended)
options.description:
✅ Deep on hierarchy, card states and overflow; brisk but real on visual system, slop risk, adaptive behaviour, accessibility and journey.
✅ Accessibility gets covered — a modifier-held HUD has genuine issues (no discoverable affordance for ←/→ or Esc, VoiceOver on a non-key panel).
❌ Longest session of the three; some passes will produce one finding each. (human: ~2h / CC: ~20min)

options.label: The three that matter
options.description:
✅ Hierarchy, interaction/card states, and overflow behaviour — where every real decision for this surface lives.
✅ Fastest route to a plan you can build from.
❌ Leaves contrast floors and keyboard/VoiceOver affordances unreviewed, and those are exactly the things that get discovered post-ship.

options.label: States + slop risk only
options.description:
✅ Narrowest useful pass: every card state specified, plus a check that the rail doesn't read as a generic AI card grid.
✅ Good if you already know how you want the layout to behave.
❌ Skips hierarchy (what a card shows first) and overflow, so the two decisions that change the layout itself stay open.

questions.question:
D3 — Generate visual mockups for the rail? <gstack-qid:plan-design-review-mockups>

ELI10: The gstack designer is available and normally I'd just generate mockups — design review without visuals is opinion. The wrinkle here is what it's good at: it produces web-flavoured mockups from a text brief, and this surface is a native macOS HUD floating over a terminal app with a themed palette. A generic mockup could actively mislead. But I have real screenshots of the running app from today's QA, so I can either feed those in as the visual context or hand-build an HTML mock that uses the app's actual token values.

Stakes if we pick wrong: no visuals and the card-layout decisions stay verbal, which is how "clean, modern card" ships. Wrong visuals and we design toward a web aesthetic the app doesn't have.

Recommendation: A — mockups grounded in the real app screenshot, so what we compare looks like Workroom rather than a landing page.

Note: options differ in kind, not coverage — no completeness score.

Net: see three concrete rails side by side, versus arguing about card layout in prose.

options.label: Grounded variants (recommended)
options.description:
✅ Three rail directions generated with a brief carrying the real token values (bg/panel/border/accent), card size, and today's app screenshot as visual reference.
✅ Comparison board with ratings and comments, so the choice is recorded as an artifact rather than a chat message.
❌ Image generation may still drift toward web conventions; I'd treat the output as layout comparison, not pixel spec. (human: ~1h / CC: ~10min)

options.label: Hand-built HTML mock
options.description:
✅ I write the rail markup myself using the app's exact tokens, real workroom names, and the true card size — pixel-honest, no model drift.
✅ Same comparison-board flow for rating the variants.
❌ Slower per variant and only as imaginative as my own layout instincts; no outside visual ideas.

options.label: Skip mockups
options.description:
✅ Straight into the seven passes; every finding lands as plan text.
✅ Nothing to discard if the layout changes once real thumbnails exist.
❌ Card layout and cursor treatment stay verbal, which is the weakest way to decide a visual surface — and the plan is already 5/10 for exactly that reason.

## Pass 1 — Information Architecture: **4/10**

The mock settles this one. Look at direction A and B: the thumbnail owns ~75% of each card, and it carries **almost no information** — a terminal pane screenshot at 220×140 is a near-blank white rectangle, because terminal content clusters in the top-left and the rest is empty. Meanwhile the thing you actually read at ⌥Tab speed — the workroom name — is 11.5pt at the bottom. The plan inverts the hierarchy: biggest element, least information.

Direction C (no thumbnails) is a third of the height and the names read instantly. The diff card is the counter-example — `+411 −222` in colour is genuinely informative at any size, and so is a live agent line ("Reading AppStore.swift…").

Board is live with all five images (three directions, the card-states row, the overflow row):

questions.question:
D5 — 1A: which rail direction is the reference? <gstack-qid:plan-design-review-direction>

Project/branch: workroom on `joel/quick-switcher-mru`, PR2's rail. The board collected no submission, so picking from the images above.

ELI10: This decides the card's information hierarchy — what your eye lands on first when the rail appears. The plan currently says a 220×140 card that is mostly screenshot with a small label underneath. Rendered at real size with real tokens, that screenshot is close to empty for a terminal pane, because terminal output hugs the top-left and the rest is blank. Meanwhile the workroom name, which is what you're actually deciding on, is the smallest thing on the card. Direction C tests whether the thumbnail earns its pixels at all.

Stakes if we pick wrong: keep thumbnail-led and ⌥Tab shows a row of near-identical white rectangles — you'd pick by reading the labels anyway, so the whole capture subsystem (7 files, epoch guard, LRU) buys nothing visible. Go label-only and you lose the one case where a picture genuinely wins: telling two diff/file panes apart at a glance.

Recommendation: D — label-led hierarchy from C, with a smaller thumbnail kept as supporting evidence in B's native chrome. It keeps the screenshot where it helps and stops it dominating where it doesn't.

Completeness: A=8/10, B=8/10, C=6/10, D=10/10 — D is the only one that covers both the informative and the near-blank thumbnail case.

Maps to two of the design principles at once: subtraction default (cut what doesn't earn its pixels) and hierarchy as service (biggest element should carry the most information).

Net: keep the picture but demote it, versus letting a blank rectangle be the loudest thing on screen.

✅ Strongest muscle-memory match to ⌘Tab: dark translucent slab, dimmed app behind, labels under each card.

content.text:
## Pass 2 — Interaction State Coverage: **3/10**

Direction D has an immediate consequence the plan hasn't reckoned with: at ~72×56 the thumbnail **cannot show text**. The plan's live `readCommandRegion` text-preview card was sized for 220×140; at 72×56 it's grey mush. So the no-snapshot state needs redesigning, not just shrinking.

Missing states, all visible in the card-states row: no-snapshot (the most common first-run card), dimmed capture (`shouldDim` baked into the pixels for a co-displayed non-focused workroom), odd-aspect split pane, content panes, the in-flight *creating* workroom (`displayedWorkroomTargets` includes it), and an item that dies mid-session.

questions.question:
D6 — 2A: at 72×56 a text preview is illegible. What does a card with no snapshot show? <gstack-qid:plan-design-review-no-snapshot>

Project/branch: workroom on `joel/quick-switcher-mru`, PR2 rail, direction D.

ELI10: A pane you haven't looked at since launch has no screenshot, because capture only happens while a pane is visible. That's the card most people see on their very first ⌥Tab. The plan's answer was "render two or three lines of live terminal text instead" — which worked at 220×140, but direction D's thumbnail is 72×56, where 6pt text is a grey smudge. So the fallback has to become something legible at thumb size.

Stakes if we pick wrong: the first impression of the feature is a row of grey smudges that look broken rather than empty — and worse, indistinguishable from a real-but-blank terminal capture, so you can't tell "nothing here yet" from "nothing running".

Recommendation: A — a kind glyph in an accent-tinted well, with the *subtitle* carrying the live text instead. The subtitle is 11pt and always legible, so the live information survives at a size where a picture cannot.

Completeness: A=10/10, B=7/10, C=8/10.

Maps to "empty states are features": this is the rail's empty state, and giving it a glyph plus a real status line is warmth, not a shrug.

Net: put the live information where it can actually be read, versus shrinking a preview until it says nothing.

options.label: Glyph well + live text in the subtitle (recommended)
options.description:
✅ Thumbnail slot shows the pane-kind SF Symbol (`terminal` / `plusminus` / `doc.text` / `clock`) centred in a `tokens.accentSoft` well — unmistakable at 72×56 and identical in light and dark.
✅ The subtitle carries the live line — `readCommandRegion`'s last non-blank command ("npm test · 248 passed", "claude · reading AppStore.swift") at 11pt, which is legible and more useful than a picture of it.
✅ Costs no capture at all, so first-run looks deliberate before any snapshot exists. (human: ~2h / CC: ~15min)
❌ Two different thumbnail treatments (photo vs glyph well) must sit side by side in one rail without looking inconsistent — needs the same corner radius and inset to hold together.

options.label: Skeleton shimmer until captured
options.description:
✅ Signals "a picture is coming" honestly, and matches the loading idiom users know from every modern app.
✅ One treatment for both cases, so no visual inconsistency in the rail.
❌ For a pane never visible this launch the picture is NEVER coming — so the shimmer lies indefinitely, which is worse than an empty state that admits what it is.

options.label: Collapse the thumbnail slot entirely
options.description:
✅ Maximum subtraction: no snapshot, no slot — the card becomes label-only and narrower, so the rail packs more items in.
✅ Zero risk of a misleading placeholder.
❌ Cards then have two different widths in one rail, which reads as a layout bug, and the cursor ring jumping between sizes draws the eye to the wrong thing.

questions.question:
D7 — 2B: how does a pane capture fit a 72×56 slot? <gstack-qid:plan-design-review-thumb-fit>

Project/branch: workroom on `joel/quick-switcher-mru`, PR2 rail, direction D.

ELI10: Panes are all sorts of shapes — a wide solo pane, a tall half of a vertical split, a whole split tree. The slot is a fixed 72×56. Something has to give: either you shrink the whole pane and accept empty bars beside it, or you crop part of it away. In the card-states row you can see the letterboxed tall split — a grey field with a white sliver — which is the ugly end of one choice. The other choice, cropping to the top-left where terminal text actually lives, looks richer but shows a zoomed fragment that isn't where you left off.

Stakes if we pick wrong: crop-zoom and two different panes can produce identical-looking thumbnails (both showing a prompt line), so the picture actively misleads. Letterbox and a tall split pane looks like a rendering bug.

Recommendation: A — aspect-fit the whole pane into the well on `tokens.surface`. At this size the thumbnail's honest job is "which pane is this, roughly" — shape, split layout, theme — not "read the output". The subtitle already carries the readable status after decision 2A.

Completeness: A=10/10, B=8/10, C=7/10.

Maps to "trust is earned at the pixel level": a thumbnail that shows a fragment out of context is a small lie, and this rail is a navigation aid where being wrong costs a switch.

Net: an honest miniature of the whole pane, versus a prettier fragment that can misidentify it.

options.label: Aspect-fit whole pane (recommended)
options.description:
✅ Never crops — the miniature always represents the entire pane, so a split reads as a split and a solo pane as a solo pane.
✅ Letterbox bars fill with `tokens.surface`, the same wash as the glyph well, so fitted and glyph cards sit together as one family.
✅ Trivial to implement and to unit-test (one `aspectRatio(contentMode: .fit)`), and identical in light and dark. (human: ~30min / CC: ~5min)
❌ A tall split pane becomes a thin sliver with wide bars — honest but visually weak; mitigate by using the whole workroom rect for workroom cards, where aspect is closer to the slot.

options.label: Crop to the pane's top-left region
options.description:
✅ Shows actual glyph shapes rather than a smear, so a busy pane looks busy and an idle one looks idle.
✅ Matches where terminal content actually lives, so the pixels carry the most information per square point.
❌ A zoomed fragment can make two different panes look identical, and for a diff pane the top-left is often just an unchanged file header.

options.label: Fill and centre-crop
options.description:
✅ No letterbox bars ever — every thumbnail is a full, edge-to-edge rectangle, which looks the tidiest in a row.
✅ One rule for every aspect, nothing special-cased.
❌ Centre-cropping a terminal throws away exactly the top-left region where the content is, so the busiest panes render as blank middles.

content.text:
## Pass 3 — User Journey: **6/10** (was going to be 3, decision 2A already fixed the worst)

The 5-second visceral moment is your *first ever* hold: only the currently-visible pane has a snapshot, so the rail is one photo plus N glyph wells. With 2A that now reads as deliberate rather than broken — before it would have been a row of grey smudges.

Remaining journey gap: **nobody discovers this feature.** ⌥Tab appears in the Keyboard Shortcuts sheet (stage 1 shipped that row) and nowhere else. The app already has `WhatsNewSheet` machinery for exactly this. Carrying that to the TODO round rather than spending a decision on it here.

5-minute behavioural moment is covered by existing feedback: the workroom chip highlights and the window title changes on commit.

## Pass 4 — AI Slop Risk: **8/10**

Classifier: **APP UI**. No hard rejections trigger — rejection #7 ("app UI made of stacked cards instead of layout") doesn't apply because here the card *is* the interaction, which the App UI rules explicitly permit. Litmus: cards necessary — yes; one job per section — yes; premium without decorative shadows — yes (one elevation, `sidebarCard(elevated:)`); motion improves hierarchy — pending Pass 7.

Two notes, not findings: the emoji in my mock (🕐 📄) stand in for SF Symbols — the real cards use `clock` / `doc.text` / `plusminus` / `terminal`, and blacklist item #7 (emoji as design elements) would apply if they shipped literally. And blacklist item #11 (`-apple-system` as primary font) is a web rule that doesn't transfer to native macOS chrome — SF Pro is the correct typeface here, and deviating would be the actual mistake.

## Pass 5 — Design System Alignment: **5/10**

Direction D settles the big one (native chrome, themed tokens — the rail won't be the only surface in the app ignoring the ghostty theme). No `DESIGN.md` remains a real gap; `/design-consultation` is the fix, but not today's job. One unresolved system decision:

questions.question:
D8 — 5A: does anything behind the rail get dimmed? <gstack-qid:plan-design-review-scrim>

Project/branch: workroom on `joel/quick-switcher-mru`, PR2 rail, direction D (themed panel, ~200×88 cards).

ELI10: The rail is a small light panel floating over your window while you hold ⌥. Nothing in the plan says what happens to everything behind it. Every OS switcher separates itself from the content somehow — ⌘Tab darkens its own slab against the desktop. Direction B, which we're building on, has no separation at all: a light panel on a light window, held apart only by a hairline border and a shadow. That reads fine over a dark terminal theme and can vanish over a light one.

Stakes if we pick wrong: no separation and on a light theme the rail's edges dissolve into the window behind it — you lose the sense that this is a transient overlay, and the cursor ring becomes the only thing your eye can lock onto. Over-dim and a navigation aid you hold for 300ms flashes the whole screen dark, which feels heavy and fights the app's calm surface hierarchy.

Recommendation: A — no full-screen dim, but give the panel real material separation: vibrancy behind it plus the existing `tokens.panel.opacity(0.7)` wash, which is the app's own recipe for a floating translucent surface (`sidebarCard(vibrant:)`, used by the inspector reveal).

Completeness: A=10/10, B=9/10, C=6/10.

Maps to the App UI rule "calm surface hierarchy, minimal chrome" — separation by material, not by darkening the user's work.

Net: separate the rail with the app's own vibrancy recipe, versus darkening the screen for a 300ms gesture or letting the panel dissolve into the window.

options.label: Vibrancy + panel wash, no dim (recommended)
options.description:
✅ `VisualEffectView` + `tokens.panel.opacity(0.7)` — the exact recipe `sidebarCard(vibrant: true)` already uses for the inspector reveal, so the rail reads as the same class of floating surface users have seen.
✅ Nothing behind changes, so a held-modifier gesture costs no visual disruption and the terminal you're leaving stays readable.
✅ Works in both light and dark themes without a second tuning pass. (human: ~1h / CC: ~10min)
❌ Over a busy pane the translucent panel picks up noise from behind it — needs the shadow and hairline to stay, and a check on the lightest bundled theme.

options.label: Soft dim behind the panel only
options.description:
✅ Strongest separation: a `DialogOverlayStyle.backdropOpacity` scrim (0.08 light / 0.25 dark) makes the rail unmistakably a transient overlay.
✅ Reuses a constant the app already ships, so the dim matches the New/Open Workroom dialogs exactly.
❌ The rail can appear for as little as 250ms; flashing a scrim on and off for a tap-and-hold reads as heavier than the action deserves, and the titlebar accessory can't be covered by it anyway.

options.label: Opaque panel, no material, no dim
options.description:
✅ Simplest and cheapest — flat `tokens.bg` with a hairline border, zero blur cost, perfectly crisp text.
✅ No risk of background noise bleeding through the panel on a busy pane.
❌ On a light theme a light opaque panel over a light window is held apart only by a 1pt border and a shadow, so the overlay reads as part of the page rather than above it.

content.text:
## Pass 6 — Responsive & Accessibility: **3/10**

"Responsive" here means item count, not viewport. Even at direction D's 200pt cards, 12 workrooms need ~2,500pt and a 1440pt screen fits about seven. The overflow row in the mock shows the plan's current answer — scroll with an edge fade and a "+4" — and it has a specific problem: **you cannot scroll a rail while holding a modifier.** There's no scrollbar, no drag, no wheel intent; items beyond the fade exist but are unreachable except by stepping the cursor blindly toward them.

Accessibility gaps I'll write into the plan alongside whatever you pick: a contrast floor for the cursor ring via `ThemeTokens.legible(accent, on: panel, target: 3.0)` (a themed accent can sit close to `panel` and the ring is the only selection signal); `.help()` tooltips on every badge and indicator per your standing rule; and VoiceOver — a panel with `canBecomeKey == false` can never hold VO focus, so each cursor move must post `NSAccessibility.post(element:, notification: .announcementRequested)` with the card's label, or the rail is silent to a screen reader.

questions.question:
D9 — 6A: 12 workrooms don't fit. Shrink, scroll, or wrap? <gstack-qid:plan-design-review-overflow>

Project/branch: workroom on `joel/quick-switcher-mru`, PR2 rail, direction D.

ELI10: With seven or so cards the rail fills the screen width. You can have twelve workrooms open. Three ways out: make the cards narrower until they all fit, keep them full-size and scroll horizontally, or wrap onto a second row. The catch with scrolling is that you're holding a modifier down — there's no scrollbar to grab, no wheel gesture that makes sense, so anything past the edge is invisible until you step the cursor toward it and hope. The mock's overflow row shows exactly that: an edge fade and a "+4" for items you can't see.

Stakes if we pick wrong: scroll and a user with twelve workrooms can't see four of them at the moment they're choosing — the rail stops being "what's open" and becomes "some of what's open". Shrink too far and the workroom names truncate to uselessness, which for a label-led card is the whole content gone.

Recommendation: A — shrink card width to fit down to a 140pt floor, then wrap to a second row. Everything on screen, always, and the name never truncates below readable.

Completeness: A=10/10, B=6/10, C=9/10.

Maps to "constraint worship" and hierarchy as service: the rail's one job is to show what you can switch to, so hiding items to preserve card size inverts the priority.

Net: always show every item, versus preserving card size at the cost of hiding some.

options.label: Shrink to a 140pt floor, then wrap (recommended)
options.description:
✅ Every open item is always visible, so ⌥Tab is a complete inventory rather than a window onto one — no blind stepping toward off-screen cards.
✅ Width interpolates between 200pt and a 140pt floor (thumbnail stays 72×56, the label column absorbs the loss), so names stay readable at every count.
✅ Second row only appears past the floor, which in practice means roughly ten-plus items — rare, and it still centres cleanly. (human: ~4h / CC: ~30min)
❌ Two layout modes to implement and test instead of one, and the cursor's ←/→ wrap has to cross rows sensibly rather than jumping visually.

options.label: Scroll with edge fade + count
options.description:
✅ One layout, fixed card size, simplest possible implementation — exactly what the plan already says.
✅ `.scrollTo(cursor, anchor: .center)` keeps the cursor visible as you step, so nothing is unreachable by keyboard.
❌ With a modifier held there's no scroll affordance at all, so items past the fade are invisible while you're deciding — and mouse users can't reach them without releasing the key.

options.label: Always two rows past N items
options.description:
✅ Full 200pt cards always — no width interpolation, so a card looks identical at 3 items and at 12.
✅ Simpler than A: one threshold, one alternate layout, no floor arithmetic.
❌ The rail's height doubles the moment you cross the threshold, so the overlay's footprint changes dramatically between sessions — and at 12 items a two-row grid starts reading as a picker, not a switcher.

content.text:
Taken: **one row, always. Shrink to fit, then scroll — ←/→ step and scroll the cursor into view, and trackpad/mouse horizontal scroll works too.** That's a real affordance a held modifier doesn't block (two-finger swipe still works), which was my objection to plain scrolling — resolved.

**Prior learning applied: `macapp-mask-contentshape-preserves-hits` (verified with a real mouse)** — the edge fade must be `.mask` + `.contentShape(.interaction, Rectangle())` or hover and click stop working on the cards under the ramp.

Pass 6 → **9/10**.

## Pass 7 — Unresolved Design Decisions

```
DECISION NEEDED                        | IF DEFERRED, WHAT HAPPENS
---------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------
Card hierarchy + size                  | RESOLVED (D5) — label-led, 200×88, 72×56 thumb
No-snapshot card                       | RESOLVED (D6) — glyph well + live text in subtitle
Thumbnail fit                          | RESOLVED (D7) — aspect-fit whole pane on surface
Separation from content                | RESOLVED (D8) — vibrancy + panel wash, no dim
Overflow                               | RESOLVED (D9) — one row, shrink then scroll
Cursor motion between cards            | OPEN — engineer picks a spring; it lags fast taps
Dimmed captures (shouldDim baked in)   | Cards for co-displayed workrooms look greyed vs peers
Badge over thumbnail                   | Moot after D5 — badge now sits in the label row
Discoverability beyond shortcuts sheet | → TODO round
```

Two of those need no decision: the badge moved to the label row when the thumbnail shrank, and dimmed captures get one line in the plan (re-capture the workroom rect *without* the dim by capturing while it is the focused member, else accept it — I'll write the accept-and-document version unless you object). One genuine open item:

D10 — 7A: how does the cursor move between cards? <gstack-qid:plan-design-review-cursor-motion>

Project/branch: workroom on `joel/quick-switcher-mru`, PR2 rail, direction D, one row with scroll.

ELI10: While the rail is up you step the cursor with Tab or ←/→, and the selected card's ring plus the scroll position both have to follow. The plan says "animate the ring's position" with the app's dialog spring (0.32s). The problem is speed: modifier release is detected by a 30ms poll, and a fast user taps Tab three or four times in a couple hundred milliseconds. A 0.32s spring per step means the ring is still travelling toward card 2 when you've already committed to card 4 — the animation is describing a past state at the exact moment it matters.

Stakes if we pick wrong: springy motion looks lovely in a demo at one step per second and feels broken at four, because you release the key while the ring is mid-flight and land somewhere the highlight never reached. Snapping everything is less pretty but always truthful.

Recommendation: A — ring and scroll both snap instantly; animate only the panel's own appear and dismiss. The reveal is where motion adds atmosphere; the cursor is where it adds lag.

Completeness: A=10/10, B=9/10, C=6/10.

Maps to the litmus check "does motion improve hierarchy or atmosphere?" — reveal motion does, per-step motion actively degrades it.

Net: a highlight that is always where you actually are, versus one that's prettier at slow speed and lies at fast speed.

options.label: Snap ring + scroll; animate only reveal (recommended)
options.description:
✅ The highlight is always on the card you're actually on, however fast you tap — no state where release and highlight disagree.
✅ Motion budget spent where it reads: the panel's spring appear/dismiss (`DialogOverlayStyle.revealAnimation`) plus the existing reduce-motion snap path.
✅ Nothing to tune and nothing that can lag behind the 30ms release poll. (human: ~15min / CC: ~2min)
❌ Stepping slowly feels mechanical next to the app's other springy transitions — a deliberate inconsistency that needs a comment saying why.

options.label: Snap the ring, ease the scroll ~0.15s
options.description:
✅ Highlight stays truthful while the row glides, so long rails don't teleport sideways and lose your place.
✅ 150ms is short enough to finish between typical taps, so lag is unlikely rather than guaranteed.
❌ Two motion rules for one gesture, and at four taps in 200ms the scroll still queues — needs an explicit "cancel in-flight and jump" rule to stay honest.

options.label: Spring both, as the plan says
options.description:
✅ Consistent with every other transition in the app, so the rail feels like it belongs.
✅ Looks best in a screen recording and at a relaxed one-step-per-second pace.
❌ At speed the ring trails the real cursor and you commit while it's mid-flight — the one failure mode that makes a switcher feel unreliable rather than slow.
