questions.question:
D11 — TODO: nobody discovers ⌥Tab except in the shortcuts sheet <gstack-qid:plan-design-review-todo-discoverability>

**What:** announce the quick switcher in `WhatsNewSheet` when the release that carries it ships.
**Why:** ⌥Tab and ⌃Tab are invisible — no menu item, no button, no hint anywhere in the UI. They appear only in Help ▸ Keyboard Shortcuts, which a user has to already suspect exists. A shortcut nobody knows about is a feature nobody has.
**Pros:** the app already has the machinery (`WhatsNewSheet`, `forceWhatsNew` fixture flag), so it's a content entry rather than new UI; it's the one moment users are actually reading about what changed.
**Cons:** What's New is per-release, so it only reaches existing users on upgrade — a brand-new install still never learns.
**Context:** stage 1 already added the two rows to `KeyboardShortcutsView.groups`, rendered from the stored trigger modifiers. The gap is that nothing surfaces it in the normal flow. A menu item under Go ("Last-used workroom") would also work and would show its own key equivalent, which is how most Mac apps teach a shortcut.
**Depends on:** nothing; independent of PR2.

ELI10: The feature is keyboard-only and silent. Deciding now whether teaching it is in scope, deferred, or something we do properly with a menu item.

Stakes if we pick wrong: skip it and the most useful shortcut in the app is known only to you.

Recommendation: C — add Go-menu items in PR2 instead of deferring. A menu item is how macOS teaches shortcuts: it shows the key equivalent next to the name, it makes the feature discoverable by browsing, and it costs two entries in a `Commands` body we're already editing.

Note: options differ in kind, not coverage — no completeness score.

Net: teach the shortcut the way macOS does, versus recording an intention to teach it later.

options.label: C · Add Go-menu items in PR2 (recommended)
options.description:
✅ "Last-used Workroom" / "Last-used Pane" under the Go menu, each showing its own key equivalent — macOS's native way of teaching a shortcut, discoverable by browsing rather than by reading docs.
✅ Also gives mouse users a way to trigger it at all, which currently doesn't exist.
❌ A menu item's key equivalent goes through the menu system, not our monitor — so it needs care to not double-fire or break the conditional ⌃Tab passthrough. (human: ~1h / CC: ~10min)

options.label: A · Add to TODOS.md as a What's New entry
options.description:
✅ Recorded with full context for whoever writes the release notes, at zero cost now.
✅ Keeps PR2 focused strictly on the rail.
❌ Reaches only upgrading users, never new installs, and TODOS.md doesn't exist in this repo yet so it needs creating.

options.label: B · Skip — the shortcuts sheet is enough
options.description:
✅ No extra surface, no menu-plumbing risk near the key handling we just got right.
✅ Defensible for a tool whose users are developers who read shortcut sheets.
❌ Leaves the feature effectively hidden, which is the most common way good keyboard features go unused.

input.old_string:
### Rail

`Views/SwitcherRailView.swift` — horizontal `ScrollView` + `ScrollViewReader`, `HStack(spacing: 12)`,
`.sidebarCard(cornerRadius: 16, margin: 0, elevated: true)`, revealed with
`DialogOverlayStyle.revealAnimation`, `.scrollTo(cursor, anchor: .center)`, and a
`@Environment(\.accessibilityReduceMotion)` snap path.

Card ≈ **220×140** (≈440×280 real px) — at 160×90 a downscaled terminal is illegible mush, which was
the outside voice's strongest argument against screenshots at all.
- thumbnail, or — when no snapshot exists — a **live text preview**: 2–3 tidied lines from
  `GhosttySurfaceView.readCommandRegion(maxBytes: 2_048)` (`:777`) + `TerminalCapture.tidy`, in the
  terminal font over `tokens.bg`. This is live even for hidden panes (occlusion stops rendering, not
  the terminal state machine) and needs no permission — it covers exactly what capture can't: a pane
  never visible this launch. Content panes fall back to their kind glyph (`plusminus` / `doc` /
  `clock`).
- title + subtitle from `AppStore.label(for:)`; `"Window \(windowNumber)"` as subtitle when one
  `SidebarID` appears in two windows.
- `UnreadBadge(count:)` top-trailing from `notifications.count(target:)` / `count(tab:)`.
- running dot from `TerminalTab.isRunning` / `terminals.isRunning(forTargetID:)`.
- cursor ring `strokeBorder(tokens.accent, lineWidth: 2)`; a11y ids `switcher.rail`,
  `switcher.card.<label>`.
- Text previews are synchronous main-thread libghostty reads: cursor ±3 only, lazily as the cursor
  moves, never from inside a libghostty callback.
input.new_string:
### Rail — designed in `/plan-design-review`, 2026-08-04

Reference mockups: `~/.gstack/projects/joelmoss-workroom/designs/switcher-rail-20260804/`
(`variant-B-workroom-native.png` for chrome, `variant-C-compact-strip.png` for hierarchy,
`card-states.png`, `overflow.png`, `mock.html` is editable and uses the real token values).

**The card is label-led, not thumbnail-led (D5).** Drawn at the plan's original 220×140 with real
tokens, a terminal thumbnail is a near-blank rectangle — terminal output hugs the top-left — so the
loudest element carried the least information while the workroom name, the thing you actually decide
on, was the smallest. Inverted:

```
  ┌───────────────────────────────────────┐   card 200×88 pt, shrinks to a 140 pt floor
  │ ┌────────┐  UITestProject / uitest-…  │   ← 13pt semibold, primary. Truncates tail.
  │ │ 72×56  │  npm test · 248 passed  ③ │   ← 11pt tokens.fgDim + badge + running dot
  │ └────────┘                            │
  └───────────────────────────────────────┘
     thumbnail   label column (absorbs all width loss)
```

- **Chrome:** one row inside `.sidebarCard(cornerRadius: 16, margin: 0, vibrant: true, elevated: true)`
  — `VisualEffectView` + `tokens.panel.opacity(0.7)`, the app's own floating-translucent recipe (the
  inspector reveal uses it). **No full-screen dim** (D8): a 250 ms gesture must not flash the screen,
  and separation comes from material + hairline + shadow instead. Cards are `tokens.panel` on
  `tokens.bg`, radius 10, thumbnail well radius 6 — three tiers, deliberately not one uniform radius.
- **Thumbnail well (D6, D7):** aspect-**fit** the whole pane capture on `tokens.surface`, never
  cropped — a crop-zoom can make two different panes look identical, and at this size the well's
  honest job is "which pane is this" (shape, split layout, theme), not "read the output". When no
  snapshot exists — the normal first-run case, since capture only happens while visible — the well
  shows the pane-kind SF Symbol (`terminal` / `plusminus` / `doc.text` / `clock`) on
  `tokens.accentSoft`. Same radius and inset as a photo well so the two sit together as one family.
- **Subtitle carries the live information** (this is where `readCommandRegion` moved to): the last
  non-blank command line, tidied — "npm test · 248 passed", "claude · reading AppStore.swift". Legible
  at 11pt where a 72×56 text preview would be grey mush. Diff/changeset cards use `+411 −222` in
  `tokens.diffAdd`/`diffRemove` instead; a root card uses its branch. `"Window 2"` when one
  `SidebarID` appears in two windows. Reads are synchronous main-thread libghostty calls, so: cursor
  ±3 only, lazily as the cursor moves, `maxBytes: 2_048`, never from inside a libghostty callback.
- **Badge + running dot** sit in the label row, not over the thumbnail — which also removes the
  contrast problem of an accent pill over arbitrary screenshot pixels. `UnreadBadge(count:)` from
  `notifications.count(target:)` / `count(tab:)`; dot from `TerminalTab.isRunning`.
- **Cursor:** `tokens.accentSoft` fill + `strokeBorder(tokens.accent, lineWidth: 1)`, and the accent
  must clear a 3:1 contrast floor against `tokens.panel` — run it through
  `ThemeTokens.legible(accent, on: panel, target: 3.0)`, because a themed accent can sit close to the
  panel and the ring is the only selection signal.
- **Overflow — one row, always (D9).** Card width interpolates 200 → 140 pt as the count grows (the
  label column absorbs every point; the thumbnail stays 72×56). Past the floor the row scrolls:
  ←/→ step the cursor and scroll it into view, and trackpad/mouse **horizontal** scroll works too (a
  two-finger swipe is available with a modifier held, which is what makes scrolling acceptable here).
  Edge fade to signal more, implemented as `.mask` + `.contentShape(.interaction, Rectangle())` —
  verified idiom, without the `contentShape` the cards under the ramp stop taking hover and clicks.
  **Never a second row.**
- **Motion (D10):** the cursor ring and the scroll offset both **snap**. Only the panel's appear and
  dismiss animate (`DialogOverlayStyle.revealAnimation`), with the usual `accessibilityReduceMotion`
  snap path. Rationale: release is detected by a 30 ms poll and a fast user taps Tab 3–4× in 200 ms,
  so a 0.32 s spring per step would still be travelling toward card 2 when the commit lands on card 4.
- **Accessibility:** `.help()` on every badge, dot and card (standing project rule); a11y ids
  `switcher.panel`, `switcher.rail`, `switcher.card.<label>`. A panel with `canBecomeKey == false` can
  never hold VoiceOver focus, so each cursor move must post
  `NSAccessibility.post(element:, notification: .announcementRequested)` with the card's label and
  position ("uitest-room-2, 2 of 5") or the rail is silent to a screen reader.
- **Dimmed captures, accepted and documented:** `PaneTreeView.shouldDim` dims a co-displayed
  non-focused workroom, so its capture is dimmed in the pixels. Not worth chasing — those cards read
  slightly greyer than their peers, which is not misleading.

**Invariant (prior learning `macapp-row-observes-sessions-invalidation-storm`):** no rail view may
hold an `AppStore` or `TerminalSessions`. `TerminalSessions` republishes per title/activity pulse; a
card observing it to compute "is cursor" would re-run at OSC frequency — the WORKROOM-2B hang.

**Discoverability (D11):** PR2 also adds two Go-menu items — "Last-used Workroom" and "Last-used
Pane" — so macOS teaches the shortcut the way it teaches every other one (the key equivalent renders
next to the name) and mouse-only users can reach the feature at all. Care needed: a menu key
equivalent routes through the menu system, not the monitor, so the items must not double-fire or
defeat the conditional ⌃Tab passthrough — bind the menu items to the same
`QuickSwitcher.step(_:reverse:in:)` entry point and let the monitor keep ownership of the keystroke.

This session is being continued from a previous conversation that ran out of context. The summary below covers the earlier portion of the conversation.

Summary:
1. Primary Request and Intent:

   The user pointed at **GitHub issue #132** in `joelmoss/workroom` and progressively drove it from issue → plan → reviewed plan → shipped stage 1 → QA → commit → capture spike → design review → (in flight) a Codex design critique.

   Issue #132 asks for a macOS ⌘Tab-style quick switcher in the Workroom macOS app:
   - **⌥Tab** to see and switch open **workrooms**; **⌃Tab** for open **detail panes** (terminals, diffs, files).
   - Quick tap switches to next; press-and-hold the modifier shows a screen-centred horizontal rail of **screenshots** with labels; ←/→ walk the rail; mouse hover and click supported; each item shows a notification count badge.

   Explicit user decisions along the way:
   - Rail cards use **real screenshots** (not text/glyph previews), **MRU ordering**, host must **support multiple windows**, **all-windows** scope for ⌥Tab.
   - Split delivery: **PR1 = keyboard/MRU only, PR2 = panel + rail + capture**.
   - Asked mid-review: "**are the suggested KB shortcuts conflict free?**" → led to the stored-modifier preference decision.
   - On capture triggers: "go with 1, but also refresh on theme change (not window resize)".
   - "**commit**" (done, `4266d32f`), "no need for PR. start #2" (the capture spike), and finally "**re-run codex**".
   - On rail overflow, overriding my recommendation: "**Only ever show one row. Shrink to fit. left/right keys should allow scrolling, as should the mouse horizontal scroller**".

   Standing constraints stated in project/global config and memory that must keep applying: **QA must run in fixture mode / throwaway `$HOME` and never mutate the real `~/.config/workroom`**; **never use `mcp__claude-in-chrome__*` tools — use the `/browse` skill**; **commit or push only when the user asks**; **never disable lint rules without asking**; `make app-*` targets require `dangerouslyDisableSandbox`; `gh` CLI fails inside the sandbox (use the GitHub MCP tools or disable the sandbox); `rm -rf` is blocked by the dcg guard and must not be retried.

2. Key Technical Concepts:
   - Workroom macOS app: SwiftUI + AppKit, macOS 15 target, Swift module named `Workroom`, target `WorkroomApp`.
   - `NSEvent.addLocalMonitorForEvents(matching: .keyDown)` in `AppDelegate` — runs inside `NSApp.sendEvent` before menu key-equivalent dispatch and before the focused terminal surface, so returning `nil` consumes an event app-wide.
   - `GhosttySurfaceView.isAppShortcut` — a static allowlist of app-reserved keys; every branch requires `.command`; Tab deliberately NOT added (runtime-conditional consumption can't be expressed statically).
   - Per-window `AppStore` (+ its own `TerminalSessions`), shared `ProjectStore`; `WindowRegistry.shared` as the only app-level coordinator.
   - `applyLocation` raises `isNavigatingHistory` for its whole body → recency must be recorded above that guard.
   - MRU: pure `RecencyList<ID>` value type; identity `WindowToken` (UUID, never reused) because `windowNumber` is reclaimed and `ObjectIdentifier` is a reusable address.
   - ScreenCaptureKit own-process capture: `SCShareableContent.currentProcess` (macOS 14.4+) + `SCContentFilter(desktopIndependentWindow:)` + `SCScreenshotManager.captureImage` — **verified TCC-free**.
   - libghostty/GhosttyKit 1.2.3: Metal-backed surfaces (no `cacheDisplay`), occlusion via `ghostty_surface_set_occlusion`, text reads via `readCommandRegion`/`readFullSurface`, and **no bytes emitted for ⌃Tab**.

3. Files and Code Sections:

   **Created — `macapp/WorkroomApp/Core/SwitcherRecency.swift`** (the MRU core; pure and headlessly testable):
   ```swift
   struct WindowToken: Hashable { private let raw: UUID; init() { raw = UUID() } }
   struct WorkroomSlotID: Hashable { let window: WindowToken; let sid: SidebarID }
   struct WorkroomSlot { weak var store: AppStore?; let sid: SidebarID; let target: TerminalTarget
     var id: WorkroomSlotID? { store.map { WorkroomSlotID(window: $0.windowToken, sid: sid) } } }

   struct RecencyList<ID: Hashable>: Equatable {
     private(set) var ids: [ID] = []
     static var maxEntries: Int { 200 }
     mutating func touch(_ id: ID) { … insert at 0, trim to maxEntries }
     mutating func forget(_ id: ID); mutating func retain(_ live: Set<ID>)
     func ordered<T>(_ items: [T], id: (T) -> ID) -> [T]   // MRU first, untouched appended positionally
   }

     static let shared = SwitcherRecency()
     private(set) var workrooms = RecencyList<WorkroomSlotID>()
     private(set) var panes = RecencyList<TerminalTab.ID>()
     func recordWorkroom(store: AppStore, sid: SidebarID?)
     func recordPane(_ id: TerminalTab.ID?)
     func forgetPanes(_ ids: [TerminalTab.ID])
     func workroomOrder(_ slots: [WorkroomSlot]) -> [WorkroomSlot]
     func paneOrder(_ tabs: [TerminalTab]) -> [TerminalTab]
   }
   ```

   **Created — `macapp/WorkroomApp/Core/QuickSwitcher.swift`**:
   ```swift
   enum QuickSwitcherKind: Equatable { case workrooms, panes }
   enum SwitcherGate { case passThrough, swallow, act(AppStore) }
   enum SwitcherModifier: String, CaseIterable, Defaults.Serializable {
     case option, control, commandOption, commandControl
     var flags: NSEvent.ModifierFlags { … }; var display: String { … }

     static let tabKeyCode: UInt16 = 48

       paneModifier: SwitcherModifier = Defaults[.switcherPaneModifier]

   }

     @discardableResult static func step(_ kind:reverse:in:registry:recency:) -> Bool
     static func workroomSlots(registry:recency:) -> [WorkroomSlot]   // filters !hasModalPresentation

   ```swift

   }
   ```

   **Modified — `macapp/WorkroomApp/Core/WindowRegistry.swift`**: `didBecomeKeyNotification` observer now also calls `SwitcherRecency.shared.recordWorkroom(store: store, sid: store.selectedTargetID)`.

   **Modified — `macapp/WorkroomApp/WorkroomApp.swift`**: refreshed the stale AppDelegate doc comment; added `switcherGate(for:in:)`:
   ```swift
   @MainActor static func switcherGate(for window: NSWindow?, in registry: WindowRegistry = .shared) -> SwitcherGate {
     guard let store = registry.store(for: window) else { return .passThrough }
     return store.hasModalPresentation ? .swallow : .act(store)

   ```

   ```swift
   if let hit = QuickSwitcherKey.classify(keyCode: event.keyCode, flags: flags) {
     if event.isARepeat { return nil }
     return MainActor.assumeIsolated {
       switch Self.switcherGate(for: window) {

Now contains Context, Stage 1 (shipped), Stage 2 spec with the designed rail, Files, Failure modes, Tests, Implementation Tasks (T1–T15), Worktree parallelization, NOT in scope, What already exists, **Approved Mockups**, Verification, Risks, and `## GSTACK REVIEW REPORT` as the terminal heading ending with `**UNRESOLVED DECISIONS:**` + one bullet (4 from prior CEO review).

Codex ran clean this time (10k tokens, no timeout).

**CODEX SAYS (design critique):**

> Classification: **APP UI**
>
> ## Findings the prior review missed
>
> 1. **The 140 pt floor is geometrically unusable.** A 72 pt preview plus padding and gap leaves roughly 40–50 pt for the name, subtitle, badge, and status dot. Names become fragments and badges collide. **Result:** the densest state becomes the least scannable. **Fix:** begin scrolling around 180–190 pt, or switch to a compact variant with a 40 pt preview/icon. Never squeeze this layout to 140 pt.
> 2. **Modifier-only activation will flash during ordinary keyboard use.** Option is used for symbols and word navigation; Control is used for navigation and shortcuts. **Result:** constant accidental panel appearances and intercepted keystrokes. **Fix:** reveal only after Tab/arrow, or after a short hold threshold; never commit unless the cursor actually moved.
> 3. **Control and Option conflict directly with VoiceOver.** Control–Option is VoiceOver's primary modifier. Announcements do not solve an invocation conflict. **Result:** the switcher disrupts assistive navigation and may announce a rapid queue after the user has already committed. **Fix:** disable modifier-only triggers under VoiceOver, provide a configurable chord/menu command, and expose a genuinely focusable accessibility model.
> 4. **Hover can silently change the selection at appearance time.** The panel may open underneath a stationary pointer and immediately select whichever card happens to be there. **Result:** releasing the modifier commits an unintended destination. **Fix:** ignore hover until physical pointer movement exceeds a small threshold after presentation.
> 5. **Tooltips are useless in this interaction.** Users are holding a modifier and committing within milliseconds; VoiceOver cannot focus the panel. **Result:** unread badges and the 6 pt dot remain unexplained. **Fix:** put state in visible text and accessibility labels/announcements. Do not rely on hover help.
> 6. **The primary identifier is allocated the weakest space.** Tail truncation removes the distinguishing end of similar workroom and branch names, exactly where collisions occur. **Result:** users select by position or screenshot guesswork. **Fix:** use structured labels with the unique segment preserved—middle truncation, compacted path components, or separate stable workroom and pane labels.
> 7. **Dynamic status has displaced stable identity.** "claude · reading…" changes continuously, while pane kind and window identity can disappear. **Result:** cards visually churn and identical panes cannot be distinguished reliably. **Fix:** always show a stable secondary identifier; treat live activity as tertiary metadata.
> 8. **The panel viewport is undefined.** "Past that the row scrolls" does not specify the maximum width, safe-area clamping, or whether alignment follows the window. **Result:** inconsistent geometry across small displays, Stage Manager, notched screens, and off-centre windows. **Fix:** define a maximum viewport width, clamp to `visibleFrame`, and centre over the key window rather than the entire screen.
> 9. **Screenshots create an information-exposure feature.** Terminal and diff previews can reveal tokens, customer data, private paths, or unreleased code during screen sharing. **Result:** invoking navigation leaks content the user did not intend to surface. **Fix:** add a preview-disable setting, sensitive-pane suppression, and an icon-only privacy mode; never persist snapshots unencrypted.
> 10. **Contrast coverage stops at the cursor.** Vibrancy, a translucent theme wash, dim text, green/red values, and 8–10% fills can fail under arbitrary Ghostty themes. **Result:** labels and state indicators disappear even though the cursor border passes 3:1. **Fix:** enforce contrast floors for every text and indicator role, with an opaque fallback surface when the theme cannot satisfy them.
>
> **Hard rejection: NONE.**

**Litmus scorecard**

| Check | Claude | Codex | Consensus |
|---|:--:|:--:|:--:|
| 1. Brand/product unmistakable first screen | YES | NO | **split** |
| 2. One strong visual anchor | YES | YES | ✅ |
| 3. Understandable by scanning labels only | YES | NO | **split** |
| 4. Each section one job | YES | YES | ✅ |
| 5. Cards actually necessary | YES | YES | ✅ |
| 6. Motion improves hierarchy | YES | YES | ✅ |
| 7. Premium without decorative shadows | YES | YES | ✅ |

5/7 agree. Both splits trace to findings 6+7 — Codex thinks the label column can't do its job at the sizes and truncation the spec gives it. That's the same complaint as finding 1, from three angles.

**Triage:**

- **#2 already satisfied** — misread of the spec. Session opens on ⌥**Tab**, not on modifier-hold; reveal is 250 ms after that keypress. Codex's own prescribed fix ("reveal only after Tab") is what's designed. Its second half ("never commit unless the cursor moved") is wrong for us — the single-tap flip *is* the feature.
- **Folding without asking** (6 items, all cheap, no decision to make): #4 hover ignored until the pointer physically moves post-reveal; #5 keep `.help()` per the standing rule but state must live in visible text + a11y announcements, never only in a tooltip; #6 preserve the unique segment — drop the shared project prefix, middle-truncate what's left; #8 max viewport width + clamp to `visibleFrame` + centre over the key **window**; #9 note that snapshots are memory-only and never persisted (opt-out already exists), sensitive-pane suppression → NOT in scope; #10 run every text and indicator role through `legible()`, not just the accent ring.
- **Three need your call** — one of them contradicts an instruction you already gave me.

- **Cursor:** `tokens.accentSoft` fill + `strokeBorder(tokens.accent, lineWidth: 1)`, and the accent
  must clear a 3:1 contrast floor against `tokens.panel` — run it through
  `ThemeTokens.legible(accent, on: panel, target: 3.0)`, because a themed accent can sit close to the
  panel and the ring is the only selection signal.
- **Contrast floors for every role, not just the cursor (D14).** Vibrancy + `panel.opacity(0.7)` over
  an arbitrary ghostty theme can wash out any of these, and the ring passing 3:1 says nothing about
  the rest: run the name through `legible(fg, on: panel, target: 4.5)`, the subtitle through
  `legible(fgDim, on: panel, target: 4.5)` (11pt body text, so 4.5 not 3.0), the running dot and the
  diff numbers through `legible(_, on: panel, target: 3.0)`, and the badge label against its own pill
  fill. If a theme can't satisfy the text floors even after `legible`, the card drops vibrancy for an
  opaque `tokens.panel` fill — legibility outranks the material.
- **Overflow — one row, always (D9, floor revised to 180pt).** Card width interpolates 200 → **180** pt
  as the count grows (the label column absorbs every point; the thumbnail stays 72×56). Past the floor
  the row scrolls: ←/→ step the cursor and scroll it into view, and trackpad/mouse **horizontal**
  scroll works too (a two-finger swipe is available with a modifier held, which is what makes
  scrolling acceptable here). Edge fade to signal more, implemented as `.mask` +
  `.contentShape(.interaction, Rectangle())` — verified idiom, without the `contentShape` the cards
  under the ramp stop taking hover and clicks. **Never a second row.**
  The floor is 180 pt, **not** the 140 pt first specified (Codex #1): at 140 the label column is
  ~36 pt, which fragments every name and collides with the badge, so the densest state would have
  been the least scannable. 180 pt keeps ~76 pt of label — a readable name plus the badge — and
  simply starts scrolling sooner (~6 cards on a 1440 pt viewport rather than ~9).
- **Viewport (D15).** The rail's own width is `min(visibleFrame.width − 2 × 24, 1100)`, clamped into
  the key window's screen `visibleFrame` (so notch and menu-bar insets are respected), and centred on
  the **key window's** frame rather than the screen — then nudged back inside `visibleFrame` if that
  centring would overhang. Without this the geometry drifts across small displays, Stage Manager and
  off-centre windows.

  needs ~1 s of hover and this whole gesture lasts a few hundred ms, so **no state may exist only in a

- **VoiceOver: tap-only, no rail (D16).** When `NSWorkspace.shared.isVoiceOverEnabled`, skip the reveal
  entirely — ⌥Tab / ⌃Tab flip immediately (stage-1 behaviour) and announce the destination. Rationale
  (Codex #3): ⌃⌥ is VoiceOver's own modifier pair, an unfocusable panel is a second-class a11y model
  whatever it announces, and a fast Tab-Tab-Tab would queue announcements that land *after* the commit.
  Observe `voiceOverStatusDidChangeNotification` so toggling VoiceOver mid-session takes effect.
  The Go-menu items (D11) remain the fully-focusable path to the same operation.
- **Hover ignored until the pointer actually moves (D17).** The panel is centred, so it can appear
  *under* a stationary cursor and `.onHover` would immediately move the selection to whatever card
  landed there — release then commits a destination the user never chose (Codex #4). Record
  `NSEvent.mouseLocation` at reveal and ignore hover until it has moved > 4 pt.

content.text:
Codex design critique folded in. Plan file, review log, decisions and learnings all updated.

**What changed in the plan**

| Codex finding | Outcome |
|---|---|
| #1 140pt floor unusable | **D9 revised** — floor is 180pt |
| #7 live-only subtitle churns | **D13** — stable identity prefix, live tail truncates first |
| #3 ⌃⌥ is VoiceOver's modifier | **D16** — tap-only under VoiceOver, no rail |
| #6 tail truncation kills the unique segment | folded — drop shared project prefix, middle-truncate |
| #4 hover selects under a stationary cursor | folded — hover armed after 4pt of real movement |
| #8 viewport undefined | folded — ≤1100pt, clamped to `visibleFrame`, centred on key window |
| #10 contrast stops at the cursor | folded — 4.5:1 text / 3:1 indicators, opaque-panel fallback |
| #5 tooltips useless in a sub-second gesture | folded — `.help()` stays, but no state lives only there |
| #9 screenshots leak during screen sharing | folded — memory-only note + existing opt-out; per-pane marking → NOT in scope |
| #2 modifier-hold flashing | already satisfied — session opens on ⌥**Tab**; its "never commit unless the cursor moved" half rejected, that's the flip |

Two things worth keeping:

The **140pt objection is arithmetic, not taste** — I specified a floor without doing the label-column subtraction at that floor. 72pt well + padding leaves ~36pt for a 13pt name. The mockup at 200pt looked fine, which is exactly why it slipped through.

The **VoiceOver conflict is the one I'd have shipped**. T15 as written was "announce on every cursor move", which treats a symptom. An unfocusable panel is a second-class model no matter how well it narrates, and the announcement queue can land after the commit. Tap-only under VoiceOver is both simpler and better, and it costs nothing — it's stage 1's behaviour, already built and tested.

Stage 1 remains committed at `4266d32f` and untouched. T7 (`AppStore.label(for:)`) is still the one open PR2 prerequisite — and D12's truncation rule now belongs in that hoisted label, so it grew slightly.

T7 done. **56/56 tests pass**, build and lint clean.

The interesting part: T7 said "two duplicate `fullTitle` copies". There were **three** — `AppStore.notificationSource` was the third, and it had already drifted. The tab chip rendered `"p/fox"`; the split title bar and notifications rendered `"p / fox"`. That's the DRY argument making itself.

**What landed**

`Core/WorkroomLabel.swift` — pure, no store:

```swift
struct WorkroomLabel: Equatable {
  let project: String      // directory name
  let workroom: String?    // label-aware displayName; nil for a root
  let branch: String?      // root's ref; nil for a workroom AND while unresolved

  static let separator = " / "
  var full: String            // "platform / fix-auth"
  var distinguishing: String  // "fix-auth" — a root's is its project, never its branch
  static func railTitles(_:) -> [String]   // D12
}
```

`AppStore.label(for: SidebarID)` resolves the parts; all four surfaces format through the one type. The chip's tooltip picks up the spaces — the two-against-one majority won.

Two things the type deliberately encodes rather than leaves to callers:

**`branch` is a field, not part of the title.** The plan flagged that `RootPresentation.make` returns a branch name and a root card must not use it as a title. Making it a separate field means no caller *can* get that wrong, and it's exactly the slot D13's subtitle needs.

**It stays nil while the ref is unresolved.** `RootPresentation.make(.unresolved)` renders the string `"root"` — a placeholder, not a branch. Passing that through as a branch name would have shown a fake branch on every root card before its ref resolved. Pinned by `testLabelForRootCarriesBranchButNotInTheTitle`.

`railTitles` is where D12 lives: one project on the rail drops the shared prefix, two or more keep it, so two `fox` workrooms in different projects never both read "fox". Middle truncation stays a view concern, documented on the function.

**PR2's prerequisites are now clear.** T9 (reducer) is the next real step — reducer + 250 ms reveal + 30 ms poll, which is where the commit timing moves from press to release. Nothing committed yet; the working tree has T7's four files plus the two new ones.

**T9 done.** `Core/QuickSwitcherReducer.swift` + 29 tests. 57/57 across the switcher suites, lint clean.

Shape: 3 phases, 9 events, 5 effects, no timers or AppKit — the controller (T10) performs effects, the reducer only decides. All four load-bearing rules are named in the assertions that pin them.

Two things worth flagging:

**The tests caught a real bug.** `.commit` range-checked the index *after* `end()` had already zeroed `count`, so `(0..<0).contains(4)` was false and **every mouse click committed nil** — clicking a card would have dismissed the rail and switched nowhere. Only visible because the test asserted the returned index rather than just "session ended".

**D17 lives in the reducer, not the view.** I modelled hover arming as state (`hoverArmed` + an `armHover` event) instead of leaving it to `SwitcherRailView`. Codex's finding was a correctness rule — the panel can appear under a stationary pointer and release then commits a card the user never chose — and rules like that belong somewhere testable. `testHoverIsIgnoredUntilArmed` now covers it headlessly; the view just reports pointer movement.

Also reused `QuickSwitcher.destination` rather than adding a fourth wrap implementation, with a test asserting a held-modifier step and a tapped step agree.

**Next: T10** — the controller. That's where the reducer meets reality: the 250 ms reveal timer, the 30 ms `NSEvent.modifierFlags` poll, `didResignActive`/`willClose`/Escape observers, the 10 s ceiling, and the VoiceOver gate (D16) that bypasses sessions entirely. It needs an injected clock to stay testable, and it's the first piece that isn't pure — so it's also where I'd expect the next real bug.

feat(macapp): quick-switcher session reducer (issue #132, T9)

The pure decision core for a hold-to-reveal switcher session: 3 phases
(idle/pending/revealed), 9 events, 5 effects, no timers and no AppKit. Modelled
on `EdgeRevealReducer` — the controller (T10) owns the reveal timer, the
modifier poll and the panel, and performs whatever effect comes back, so every
transition is covered headlessly.

Four rules carry the weight, each named in the test that pins it:

  - `.idle` swallows everything, so the modifier release that inevitably
    follows a mouse click can't commit a second time.
  - a step while `.pending` reveals immediately (⌥Tab⌥Tab means "show me now").
  - `revealTimerFired` outside `.pending` is a no-op, so a timer firing after a
    fast release can't resurrect a finished session.
  - `itemsChanged(0)` ends without committing; `> 0` clamps the cursor.

D17's hover arming is modelled here rather than left to the view: the panel is
centred, so it can appear *under* a stationary pointer, and an unarmed
`.onHover` would move the selection to whatever card landed there — the release
would then commit a destination the user never chose. That's a correctness rule,
so it lives somewhere testable.

Step math calls `QuickSwitcher.destination` (which shares `AppStore.wrapped`
with both tab cyclers), so a held step and a tapped step cannot disagree.

Reveal delay is 250ms, not the 180ms first planned: 180 flashes the panel on a
chorded tap, and the 180 in `EdgeRevealSidebar` is a *hide* debounce — reading
it as precedent was a misread.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
EOF

content.text:
**T10 done** — the controller. 101/101 across every switcher and shortcut-routing suite, lint clean, uncommitted.

`Core/QuickSwitcherController.swift` + 24 tests. Every seam injected (`flagsProvider`, `voiceOverEnabled`, `pointerProvider`, `startTimers`, `announce`, and the three rail callbacks), so none of it waits on a real 30 ms timer or needs a window on screen.

Four things worth calling out, three of which I only got right because writing the tests forced the question:

**`.common` run-loop mode is load-bearing.** The plan's argument for polling was that `NSEvent.modifierFlags` is a global hardware snapshot that survives menu tracking and Mission Control. True — but a `Timer` added in the *default* mode doesn't fire during menu tracking or a modal loop, so the poll would have stalled in exactly those cases and the rail would hang until the mode exited. `.common` includes the tracking modes.

**`willClose` reconcile is deferred one tick.** The closing window is still in `allStores` *during* the notification, so a same-tick re-resolve keeps counting the window that's going away.

**Items are frozen at open.** MRU order changes the instant anything is selected — which is what a commit does — so a live-resolved list would reshuffle under the cursor mid-gesture.

**`pointerProvider` exists because of a test I couldn't write.** D17's threshold compares the hover position against the pointer position at reveal. I'd only injected the hover side, so the comparison was against the *real* mouse — wherever the machine's cursor happened to sit when the suite ran. Both reads now go through one seam.

Also extracted `QuickSwitcher.commit(_:from:)` / `commit(pane:in:)` so the tap path and the release path share one raise-then-select ordering rather than growing a second copy.

**Next: T11** — the panel and the rail. That's the biggest remaining piece (a session's worth), and the first one that's genuinely visual: non-activating `NSPanel`, 200→180pt label-led cards, the glyph well, one-row shrink-then-scroll, and the contrast floors. The controller's three callbacks are the seam it hangs on.

feat(macapp): quick-switcher session controller (issue #132, T10)

Wires the reducer to the world: freezes the candidate list at open, polls the
trigger modifier, watches the ways a session can die, and performs the commit.
The panel is deliberately not owned here — onReveal/onCursorMoved/onEnd are the
seam the rail (T11) hangs on, which keeps the whole class testable with no
window on screen.

Release detection is a 30ms poll of `NSEvent.modifierFlags`, not a
`flagsChanged` monitor: a global hardware snapshot stays true through menu
tracking, Mission Control and another app holding focus, all of which starve a
local monitor — and it avoids the footgun that a `flagsChanged` monitor must
always return the event or `GhosttySurfaceView` leaves libghostty believing ⌥ is
still held.

The `.common` run-loop mode on those timers is load-bearing. The default mode
does not run during menu tracking or a modal loop, so a `.default` poll would
stall in exactly the cases the hardware snapshot exists to survive, and the rail
would hang until the mode exited.

Three more things that are easy to get wrong:

  - items are frozen at open, because MRU order changes the instant anything is
    selected — which is what a commit does — so a live-resolved list would
    reshuffle under the cursor mid-gesture.
  - the `willClose` reconcile is deferred one tick: the closing window is still
    in `allStores` during the notification, so a same-tick re-resolve keeps
    counting the window that is going away.
  - the trigger modifier is read from `Defaults` per kind, so the poll watches
    the configured chord and a partial chord (⌘ released from ⌘⌃) counts as a
    release.

D16: with VoiceOver running this opens no session at all. ⌃⌥ is VoiceOver's own
modifier pair, a panel that cannot become key can never hold VoiceOver focus
however well it narrates, and a fast Tab-Tab-Tab would queue announcements that
land after the commit — so it degrades to the stage-1 tap flip and announces
where it landed.

Escape and ←/→ join the monitor, consumed only while a session is live. Plain
arrows only: the tab cyclers carry ⌘, so a held-⌥ rail cannot collide with them.

`QuickSwitcher.commit(_:from:)` / `commit(pane:in:)` are extracted from the two
step functions so the tap path and the release path share one raise-then-select
ordering rather than growing a second copy.

input.command:
git status --short; echo "---"; git add -A && git commit -q -F - <<'EOF'
feat(macapp): quick-switcher panel and label-led rail (issue #132, T11)

The rail: one row of label-led cards in a non-activating floating panel. Three
pieces — `SwitcherRailLayout` (pure geometry + contrast), `SwitcherPanel` (the
window), `SwitcherRailView` (the SwiftUI rail) — so the parts that fail silently
on someone else's display or theme are unit-tested rather than eyeballed.

Label-led, not thumbnail-led: at the originally-planned 220x140 a terminal
thumbnail is a near-blank rectangle, so the loudest element carried the least
information while the name — the thing you decide on — was the smallest.

The card floor is 180pt, not 140. At 140 the label column is ~36pt: every name
fragments and the badge collides, so the densest state would have read the worst.
Past the floor the single row scrolls; never a second row.

`SwitcherPanel.canBecomeKey` is false and load-bearing. The gesture depends on
the workroom window staying key, because the AppDelegate monitor resolves its
store from the key window — the moment this panel could take focus, ⌥Tab would
stop working as soon as the rail appeared. `isOpaque = false` is equally
load-bearing: `NSWindow.occlusionState` counts only opaque coverage, so an opaque
rail would convince every terminal behind it that it was occluded and stop it
rendering. Both have tests.

Two bugs found while verifying this live, both worth knowing:

  - **A launch crash (SIGSEGV in `Color._apply`).** `NSColor(someSwiftUIColor)`
    yields a lazily-resolved, SwiftUI-backed colour whose `usingColorSpace`
    returns nil outside a view update — so the contrast helper's guard silently
    handed it back unchanged, and re-wrapping THAT in a `Color` crashed during
    the first window's layout, since the pre-created panel's hosting view shares
    the app's attribute graph. `Palette` now resolves in `NSColor` throughout
    with `Color` accessors on top, and the two diff foregrounds gained `ns*`
    tokens. Never round-trip `Color` back through `NSColor`.
  - **Names truncated on cards wide enough to fit them twice.** A trailing
    `Spacer(minLength: 0)` is a *flexible* child, so SwiftUI split the card's
    spare width between it and the label column. `maxWidth: .infinity` on the
    labels claims that space instead.

Contrast floors cover every role, not just the cursor: 4.5:1 for the name and
subtitle (11-13pt body text), 3:1 for the ring, dot and diff numbers, and a card
whose theme cannot meet the text floor drops vibrancy for an opaque fill.
Legibility outranks the material.

**T11 done and committed.** The rail is live and verified on screen.

**121/121 tests pass, lint clean.** Four commits now: T7, T9, T10, T11.

Two real bugs found — neither by a test:

**A launch crash (SIGSEGV in `Color._apply`).** You caught this one. `NSColor(someSwiftUIColor)` returns a lazily-resolved, SwiftUI-backed colour whose `usingColorSpace` returns nil outside a view update. My contrast helper's guard silently handed it back unchanged, and re-wrapping *that* in a `Color` crashed during the **first window's** layout — because the pre-created panel's hosting view shares the app's attribute graph, so my rail's colours were being resolved before any rail existed. `Palette` now resolves in `NSColor` throughout with `Color` accessors on top. Every unit test passed with the crashing code, because the crash needs a live SwiftUI update cycle.

**Names truncated on cards wide enough to fit them twice.** Found by screenshotting the rail. A trailing `Spacer(minLength: 0)` is a *flexible* child, so SwiftUI split the card's spare width between it and the label column — `uitest-room-2` rendered as `uites...om-2`. `maxWidth: .infinity` on the labels fixes it.

Verified live in fixture mode with 4 workrooms: rail reveals, cursor ring lands on the MRU item, badge renders, glyph wells, D12's prefix-drop working (name in the title, project in the subtitle), full names now untruncated.

**One judgment call I left for you.** On a theme with a pale accent, `legible(accent, on: panel, target: 3.0)` walks the cursor ring to near-black while `UnreadBadge` keeps the raw accent — so the ring reads neutral and the two disagree. The floor is doing its job (the ring is clearly visible), but it loses the accent identity. Fixing it properly means touching the shared badge component, which is wider than this issue.

I also added `WorkroomUITestSwitcherReveal`, because a held modifier genuinely isn't drivable by synthetic input — `NSEvent.modifierFlags` is a global *hardware* snapshot, so a scripted hold never reaches it. The 250 ms delay and real-mouse hover remain manual, as the plan expected.

feat(macapp): rail thumbnails via own-window capture (issue #132, T12)

Real screenshots in the switcher rail. One window capture per shot, cropped into
N per-pane thumbnails, downscaled to the 72x56 well and cached.

No Screen Recording permission, no Info.plist key, no entitlement:
`SCShareableContent.currentProcess` returns content capturable "without user
consent via TCC", and the T1 spike confirmed the *capture* also hands back real
pixels — preflight false, no prompt, and a never-activated background window
captured fine. Verified again end-to-end here: a real terminal screenshot
renders in a card with no prompt.

The crop math is its own file with its own tests because the plan was wrong here
in two independent ways, both of which look obviously true:

    NSWindow.frame      (200, 200, 820, 552)   AppKit: y-UP,   bottom-left
    filter.contentRect  (205, 872, 810, 544)   CG:     y-DOWN, top-left, inset
    captured image       1620 x 1088  ==  contentRect x pointPixelScale, EXACTLY

`contentRect` is not the window frame — deriving the scale from the delivered
image against the frame gave 1.9756 (x) and 1.9710 (y), neither 2.0 nor equal to
each other, a ~1.2% drift that reaches ~10px by the far edge of a large window.
And the y-flips do not cancel, because `convertToScreen` is y-up while
`contentRect` is y-down. So the reference rect is always `contentRect`, the scale
is always `pointPixelScale`, and the region is flipped exactly once. The tests pin
the measured numbers: a fixture where `contentRect.size == frame.size` passes a
wrong implementation.

A mislabelled card is made structurally impossible rather than unlikely. The
epoch, the window frame and every region rect are read synchronously before the
await; if the epoch or the frame changed by the time pixels arrive, the whole
shot is discarded rather than cropped against new rects. Worst case is a stale
card, never a wrong one. A capture is also refused outright for a window that
isn't visible, is miniaturized, or is on another Space — that last one returns an
all-black *successful* image, which "keep the old entry on failure" would
cheerfully cache as the new truth.

Cache is LRU, bounded by count and bytes, with an injected clock, and treats an
older theme generation as a miss: the picture is of colours no longer on screen.
Correctness needs no purge-on-window-close hook, because `WindowToken` is a UUID
that is never reused, so a closed window's key cannot collide with a live one.

Designed degradation, now observed rather than assumed: only the selected
workroom has an on-screen region, so a workroom not visited this launch keeps its
glyph well, and the first-ever reveal shows glyphs because the capture lands after
the panel does.

**Ironic bug worth recording:** six tests failed on "no thumbnail" because my *fake capturer* handed the service an AppKit frame as `contentRect`. That's the exact y-up/y-down confusion `SnapshotGeometry` exists to prevent, reproduced inside the test meant to guard it. Production code was correct.

**Two designed degradations, now observed rather than assumed:**
- Only the *selected* workroom has an on-screen region, so cards for workrooms not visited this launch keep their glyph wells. There is nothing to photograph.
- The first-ever reveal always shows glyphs — capture is async and lands after the panel is already up. The second reveal has the picture.

Both were predicted in the plan; it's better to have watched them happen.

**Remaining:** T13 (capture trigger policy — the ~3 s per-window floor, occlusion + app-active gating, so thumbnails refresh in the background rather than only on open), T14 (Go-menu items), T15 (rail a11y + the VoiceOver gate). T13 is the one that makes thumbnails feel current rather than "whatever it was last time you held ⌥Tab".
ok, so screenshots are not working here - too small, useless. Present some alternatives that are still useful where each item is unique enough to be quickly identifiable

Fair. At 72×56 an aspect-fit window shot is a grey smudge — and the mock predicted that; I shipped the capture anyway because the plan said to.

Worth saying plainly: **A, B and C below make T12 dead code.** The snapshot layer would either be reverted or left behind `railPreviews`, off by default. Only D keeps it.

The deeper point: ⌘Tab works because app icons are **stable and learnable** — you recognise the shape before you read anything. A screenshot is neither stable (it changes every time) nor distinctive (every terminal looks like every other terminal). So the strongest alternatives replace "a picture of it" with "a mark for it".

content.text:
What would you like to clarify?

A few things I could be wrong about, in case one of them is what you're reacting to:

- Whether you want **workroom** cards and **pane** cards solved the same way. A pane's identity problem is different — four terminals in one workroom all share the branch and diffstat, so a colour-per-name mark does much less work there.
- Whether "unique enough" means *learnable over time* (a stable mark you come to recognise) or *readable right now* (enough text to tell them apart on first sight). I assumed the former and recommended accordingly.
- Whether the thumbnail should be gone entirely or just demoted. I framed it as either/or.
- Whether you'd already ruled out keeping capture at a larger size, or were open to it — I included it as an option, but you may have meant screenshots are dead full stop.
is this for workroom switching only?

No — one rail, both switchers. `SwitcherCardView` draws ⌥Tab workroom cards and ⌃Tab pane cards identically, same 72×56 well, and T12 registers snapshot regions for both (`WorkroomPaneLeaf` for workrooms, `PaneLeafView` for panes).

Which matters, because the two have **different** identity problems:

**Workrooms (⌥Tab)** — different names, branches, diffstats, badges. Text alone nearly separates them; a mark mainly buys recognition speed.

**Panes (⌃Tab)** — all inside *one* workroom, so branch, project and diffstat are identical across every card. What actually differs: kind (terminal / diff / file / commit), title (`zsh`, `nvim`, `AppStore.swift`), the running command, and position in the split. A colour-from-name mark does little here — but the kind glyph plus a filename already does a lot, and it's the case where a picture would genuinely have helped most (a diff *looks* unlike a terminal) if it were legible at all.

So "one answer for both" may be the wrong shape. Do you want:

- **One treatment for both**, accepting it's tuned for workrooms, or
- **Different treatment per switcher** — marks + VCS status for workrooms, kind glyph + filename + live command for panes?

And separately: is capture dead for **both**, or dead for workrooms but worth keeping for panes at a larger size, where the visual difference between a diff, a file and a terminal is real?
capture is dead for both. but use something visual for each pane type (diff, terminal, etc). Use different treatment per switcher

Both dead, per-switcher treatment. So T12 comes out — I'll revert the snapshot layer rather than leave it behind a flag, since nothing will ever turn it on.

Two designs to settle, one per switcher.

git add -A && git commit -q -F - <<'EOF'
feat(macapp): per-switcher card identities replace screenshots (issue #132)

Screenshots are gone (the snapshot layer is reverted in the previous commit). At
any size that fits a switcher rail an aspect-fit terminal capture is a grey
smudge, and it was never the right idea: ⌘Tab works because app icons are stable
and distinctive, and a screenshot is neither — it changes every time, and every
terminal looks like every other terminal.

The two switchers have different identity problems, so they now get different
wells:

⌥Tab workrooms get a **mark** — a colour and a monogram you learn the way you
learn an app icon. The monogram follows the displayed name so it matches what you
read; the hue follows the target id, so a relabel re-letters the tile without
moving the colour you actually recognise.

⌃Tab panes get a **miniature drawn from their own data** — a prompt chevron with
a live pip for a terminal, stacked add/remove bars for a diff, text lines for a

9	/// key window, and release detection ends the session, not a focus change.
10	final class SwitcherPanel: NSPanel {
11	  /// Load-bearing. Key focus must stay with the workroom window or the monitor's store lookup misses
12	  /// and ⌥Tab stops working the moment the rail appears.
13	  override var canBecomeKey: Bool { false }
14	  override var canBecomeMain: Bool { false }
15	}

18	/// the first `NSHostingView` render costs real milliseconds, and paying that at the 250 ms reveal is
19	/// exactly the wrong moment.
20	@MainActor
21	final class SwitcherPanelController {
22	  static let shared = SwitcherPanelController()
23	
24	  private var panel: SwitcherPanel?
25	  private let model = SwitcherRailModel()
26	  private var themeObserver: NSObjectProtocol?
27	
28	  /// Build the panel and its hosting view, ordered out. Safe to call more than once.
29	  func prepare() {
30	    guard panel == nil else { return }
31	    let panel = SwitcherPanel(
32	      contentRect: NSRect(x: 0, y: 0, width: 600, height: 120),
33	      styleMask: [.nonactivatingPanel, .borderless], backing: .buffered, defer: false)
34	    panel.isFloatingPanel = true
35	    panel.level = .floating
36	    // `.canJoinAllSpaces` so a rail opened just before a Space switch doesn't strand; `.ignoresCycle`
37	    // so ⌘` skips it (belt and braces — `isCycleableWindow` already requires `canBecomeKey`).
38	    panel.collectionBehavior = [.canJoinAllSpaces, .fullScreenAuxiliary, .ignoresCycle, .transient]
39	    // `isOpaque = false` is load-bearing and has a test. `NSWindow.occlusionState` counts only OPAQUE
40	    // coverage, so a clear panel never flips it — give this an opaque background and every terminal
41	    // surface behind the rail believes it is occluded and stops rendering.
42	    panel.isOpaque = false
43	    panel.backgroundColor = .clear
44	    panel.hasShadow = false
45	    panel.isReleasedWhenClosed = false
46	    panel.isExcludedFromWindowsMenu = true
47	    panel.animationBehavior = .none
48	    panel.ignoresMouseEvents = false
49	    panel.setAccessibilityIdentifier("switcher.panel")

60	    controller.onReveal = { [weak self] items, cursor in self?.show(items: items, cursor: cursor) }
61	    controller.onCursorMoved = { [weak self] index in self?.model.cursor = index }
62	    controller.onEnd = { [weak self] in self?.hide() }

69	    themeObserver = NotificationCenter.default.addObserver(

feat(macapp): drop shadow on the switcher rail, softer cursor ring (issue #132)

The rail sat flat on whatever was behind it. It now casts a soft drop shadow,
and the cursor ring is a hairline at a wider radius instead of a 1.5pt box.

The shadow took three measured corrections, none of which a test would have
caught:

- **The window can't cast it.** A borderless non-opaque panel produces no
  system shadow at all: with `hasShadow = true` plus `invalidateShadow()`, a
  pixel diff of the same screen with and without the panel found zero
  darkening at 6/14/26/44pt out on every side — with glass content and with a
  solid opaque fill alike. `hasShadow` stays false.
- **A clip applies to a view's background.** Mounted alongside the glass, the
  shadow was clipped away entirely; it goes on after `clipShape`.
- **A layer shadow on the representable didn't render either**, `shadowPath`
  and all. A SwiftUI shape's shadow does — cast by a card-coloured rounded
  rect behind the glass, so anything the glass lets through reads as the
  rail's own surface.

Because the shadow is drawn, it needs room inside the window: the panel is now
`shadowMargin` bigger than the rail slab on all four sides, and that halo is
click-through (`HaloContentView`) so it can't swallow clicks meant for the
window underneath. The margin equals `screenMargin`, so a full-width rail plus
its shadow lands exactly inside `visibleFrame` and the centring clamp never
fires. Measured after the fix: 0.13 darkening 4px below the slab decaying to
0.045 at 34px, nothing at all past the halo.

Two contrast bugs surfaced on the way, both from tests that read the *ambient*
theme and started failing on untouched code once the machine's theme
preference changed:

- `tileColor` walked brightness one way, chosen from the theme's *background*
  while the tile is measured against its *panel* — on a theme where those
  straddle mid-grey it walked toward the panel and never cleared 3:1. It now
  tries both directions, and treats saturation as a fallback axis: against a
  mid-grey card (luminance 0.186) the best a 0.62-saturated hue can reach is
  2.71:1 at any brightness, so desaturating is the only way to the floor.
- `needsOpaqueFill` keyed on the 4.5:1 text floor, so a card that caps at
  4.45:1 — 99% of the floor, no perceptible difference — threw away the whole
  Liquid Glass surface. Going opaque doesn't raise the ratio anyway; it only
  makes the measured background the real one. It now keys on its own 4.0:1
  floor.

The three ambient-theme tests now pin explicit light and dark fixtures, so a
floor no longer passes or fails depending on who runs it.

Shadowing a floating overlay window in the macapp (the ⌥Tab/⌃Tab switcher rail, issue #132) failed three ways before working. All three were found by pixel-diffing two screenshots (rail shown vs dismissed) and comparing luminance at 4/10/20/34px out — never by looking.

1. **`NSPanel.hasShadow = true` does nothing** for `[.nonactivatingPanel, .borderless]` + `isOpaque = false`. Zero darkening at every distance on every side, with `invalidateShadow()` called, and with `NSGlassEffectView` content **and** a solid opaque `CALayer` fill alike — so it is not the glass suppressing it.
2. **SwiftUI `.clipShape` clips a view's `.background` too**, so a shadow mounted in the same `.background` as the material is clipped away entirely. It must be a *second* `.background` applied AFTER the `clipShape`.
3. **A CALayer shadow with an explicit `shadowPath` on an `NSViewRepresentable` still did not render** inside `NSHostingView`. What works is a plain SwiftUI shape: `RoundedRectangle(...).fill(<opaque-ish>).shadow(...)` behind the material.

Consequences to keep in mind: a *drawn* shadow is clipped at the window's bounds, so the window must be padded beyond the visible slab (`SwitcherRailLayout.shadowMargin`), that halo must be made click-through with a `hitTest` override or it swallows clicks meant for the window below, and the halo should equal the screen-edge margin so a full-width overlay plus shadow still lands inside `visibleFrame`.

See [[macapp-settings-aux-window-gotchas]], [[pixel-perfect-ui]].

Done, verified on screen and measured. Committed as `669a0cd7`.

**Shadow.** `hasShadow = true` was the obvious move and it's a dead end — a borderless non-opaque `NSPanel` casts no system shadow at all. I pixel-diffed the same screen with and without the panel: zero darkening at 6/14/26/44pt out on every side, with `invalidateShadow()` called, with glass content *and* with a solid opaque fill, so it isn't the glass suppressing it. Two more dead ends followed: `.clipShape` clips a view's `.background`, so a shadow mounted with the glass was clipped away entirely; and a layer shadow with an explicit `shadowPath` on the representable didn't render inside `NSHostingView` either. What works is a plain SwiftUI shape shadow behind the glass, mounted *after* the clip. Measured after the fix: 0.13 darkening 4px below the slab decaying to 0.045 at 34px, heavier below than above, and nothing past the halo.

Because it's drawn, it needs room: the window is now 24pt bigger than the rail on all four sides, and that halo is click-through so it can't swallow clicks meant for the window underneath. The halo equals the screen-edge margin, so a full-width rail plus shadow still lands inside `visibleFrame` and the centring clamp never fires.

**Softer border** — I read this as the cursor ring, the only border the rail draws, which was a 1.5pt box. It's now a hairline at radius 14, nested inside the rail's 20. I deliberately didn't soften it by dropping opacity: that looks the same and quietly fails the 3:1 floor the ring is measured against. If you meant the rail's own outer edge instead, say so — that's the glass's rim and a different knob.

**Two contrast bugs fell out**, both real, neither from this change. Three tests read the *ambient* theme, so they started failing on untouched code once the machine's theme preference changed:

- `tileColor` walked brightness one direction, picked from the theme's *background*, while the tile is measured against its *panel*. Where those straddle mid-grey it walked toward the panel and never cleared 3:1. Now it tries both, and treats saturation as a fallback axis — against a mid-grey card (luminance 0.186) the best a 0.62-saturated hue can reach is 2.71:1 at *any* brightness, so desaturating is the only route to the floor.

Those three tests now pin explicit light and dark fixtures, so a contrast floor no longer passes or fails depending on who runs it. **153/153 across the switcher suites, lint clean.**

One thing to flag: while chasing this I briefly launched a QA instance that wasn't properly isolated (`open` needs `--env HOME=…`; a plain `HOME=… open` doesn't propagate), and two ⌥Tab keystrokes may have landed on your live Dev app — that would have changed which workroom was selected there, nothing more.   func applicationDidFinishLaunching(_ n: Notification) {
    let w: CGFloat = 520, h: CGFloat = 160
    panel = NSPanel(
      contentRect: NSRect(x: 0, y: 0, width: w, height: h),

        caster.wantsLayer = true

content.text:
Fixed, and it was my bug from the shadow commit. `cabcac94`.

A shadow needs an opaque caster, and I put that caster behind the glass. An opaque layer anywhere beneath an `NSGlassEffectView` doesn't dim the material — it annihilates it. Measured across a rail-sized interior over a high-contrast backdrop:

| construction | interior sd | corr. with backdrop |
|---|---|---|
| `NSGlassEffectView` alone | 0.0085 | +0.809 |
| …with a `contentView` set | 0.0085 | +0.809 |
| …inside `NSGlassEffectContainerView` | 0.0085 | +0.809 |
| `NSVisualEffectView` `.hudWindow`/`.behindWindow` | 0.0241 | −0.361 |
| glass **+ opaque layer below** | **0.0000** | **0.000** |

Zero variation, zero correlation — a flat fill. Exactly what you saw.

The caster now keeps only its spill: `destinationOut` punches its own footprint out, so the glass gets a transparent window to sample through again. The mask's rectangle is expanded by `shadowMargin`, because a mask hides whatever falls outside it and would otherwise take the spill with it. Shadow still falls off 0.141 → 0.032 over 40px, and the rail's interior now sits at 0.892 against a 0.921 backdrop instead of the black of an unmasked caster.

Two things from that run worth knowing. The three glass constructions are byte-identical, so `contentView` and `NSGlassEffectContainerView` buy nothing here — no point reaching for them. And glass genuinely flattens: it compresses backdrop variation ~3.5× and lifts a dark backdrop toward mid-grey, so over a *uniform* surface it will always look like a plain tint no matter what. If it still reads too flat on your themes, `.hudWindow` vibrancy keeps nearly all the backdrop variation (0.0241 vs 0.0299) — it's less faithful to ⌘Tab but more obviously a material. Say the word and I'll switch it.

## AskUserQuestion Format

### Tool resolution (read first)

"AskUserQuestion" can resolve to two tools at runtime: the **host MCP variant** (e.g. `mcp__conductor__AskUserQuestion` — appears in your tool list when the host registers it) or the **native** Claude Code tool.

**Conductor rule (read before the MCP rule):** if `CONDUCTOR_SESSION: true` was echoed by the preamble, do NOT call AskUserQuestion at all — neither native nor any `mcp__*__AskUserQuestion` variant. Render EVERY decision brief as the **prose form** below and STOP. This is proactive, not a reaction to a failure: Conductor disables native AUQ and its MCP variant is flaky (it returns `[Tool result missing due to internal error]`), so prose is the reliable path. **Auto-decide preferences still apply first:** if a `[plan-tune auto-decide] <id> → <option>` result has already surfaced for a question, proceed with that option (no prose). Because in Conductor you go straight to prose without ever calling the tool, this auto-decide-first ordering is enforced HERE, not only by the PreToolUse hook. When you render a Conductor prose brief, also capture it with `bin/gstack-question-log` (the PostToolUse capture hook never fires on a prose path, so `/plan-tune` history/learning depends on this call).

**Rule (non-Conductor):** if any `mcp__*__AskUserQuestion` variant is in your tool list, prefer it. Hosts may disable native AUQ via `--disallowedTools AskUserQuestion` (Conductor does, by default) and route through their MCP variant; calling native there silently fails. Same questions/options shape; same decision-brief format applies.

If AskUserQuestion is unavailable (no variant in your tool list) OR a call to it fails, do NOT silently auto-decide or write the decision to the plan file as a substitute. Follow the **failure fallback** below.

### When AskUserQuestion is unavailable or a call fails

Tell three outcomes apart:

1. **Auto-decide denial (NOT a failure).** The result contains `[plan-tune auto-decide] <id> → <option>` — the preference hook working as designed. Proceed with that option. Do NOT retry, do NOT fall back to prose.
2. **Genuine failure** — no variant in your tool list, OR the variant is present but the call returns an error / missing result (MCP transport error, empty result, host bug — e.g. Conductor's MCP AskUserQuestion is flaky and returns `[Tool result missing due to internal error]`).
   - If it was present and **errored** (not absent), retry the SAME call **once** — but only if no answer could have surfaced (a missing-result error can arrive after the user already saw the question; retrying would double-prompt, so if it may have reached them, treat as pending, don't retry).
   - Then branch on `SESSION_KIND` (echoed by the preamble; empty/absent ⇒ `interactive`):
     - `spawned` → defer to the **Spawned session** block: auto-choose the recommended option. Never prose, never BLOCKED.
     - `headless` → `BLOCKED — AskUserQuestion unavailable`; stop and wait (no human can answer).
     - `interactive` → **prose fallback** (below).

**Prose fallback — render the decision brief as a markdown message, not a tool call.** Same information as the tool format below, different structure (paragraphs, not ✅/❌ bullets). It MUST surface this triad:

1. **A clear ELI10 of the issue itself** — plain English on what's being decided and why it matters (the question, not per-choice), naming the stakes. Lead with it.
2. **Completeness scores per choice** — explicit `Completeness: X/10` on EACH choice (10 complete, 7 happy-path, 3 shortcut); use the kind-note when options differ in kind not coverage, but never silently drop the score.
3. **The recommendation and why** — a `Recommendation: <choice> because <reason>` line plus the `(recommended)` marker on that choice.

Layout: a `D<N>` title + a one-line note to reply with a letter (in Conductor this is the normal path; elsewhere it means AskUserQuestion was unavailable or errored); the issue ELI10; the Recommendation line; then ONE paragraph per choice carrying its `(recommended)` marker, its `Completeness: X/10`, and 2-4 sentences of reasoning — never a bare bullet list; a closing `Net:` line. Split chains / 5+ options: one prose block per per-option call, in sequence. Then STOP and wait — the user's typed answer is the decision. In plan mode this satisfies end-of-turn like a tool call.

**Continuation — mapping a typed reply back to a brief.** Each brief carries a stable label (`D<N>`, or `D<N>.k` in a split chain). The user references it (e.g. "3.2: B"). A bare letter maps to the single most-recent UNANSWERED brief; if more than one is open (a split chain), do NOT guess — ask which `D<N>.k` it answers. Never apply a bare letter ambiguously across a chain.

**One-way / destructive confirmations in prose.** When the decision is a one-way door (irreversible or destructive — delete, force-push, drop, overwrite), prose is a WEAKER gate than the tool, so make it stronger: require an explicit typed confirmation (the exact option letter or word), state plainly what is irreversible, and NEVER proceed on a vague, partial, or ambiguous reply — re-ask instead. Treat silence or "ok"/"sure" without the explicit choice as not-yet-confirmed.

### Format

Every AskUserQuestion is a decision brief and must be sent as tool_use, not prose — unless the documented failure fallback above applies (interactive session + the call is unavailable/erroring), in which case the prose fallback is the correct output.

```
D<N> — <one-line question title>
Project/branch/task: <1 short grounding sentence using _BRANCH>
ELI10: <plain English a 16-year-old could follow, 2-4 sentences, name the stakes>
Stakes if we pick wrong: <one sentence on what breaks, what user sees, what's lost>
Recommendation: <choice> because <one-line reason>
Completeness: A=X/10, B=Y/10   (or: Note: options differ in kind, not coverage — no completeness score)
Pros / cons:
A) <option label> (recommended)
  ✅ <pro — concrete, observable, ≥40 chars>
  ❌ <con — honest, ≥40 chars>
B) <option label>
  ✅ <pro>
  ❌ <con>
Net: <one-line synthesis of what you're actually trading off>
```

D-numbering: first question in a skill invocation is `D1`; increment yourself. This is a model-level instruction, not a runtime counter.

ELI10 is always present, in plain English, not function names. Recommendation is ALWAYS present. Keep the `(recommended)` label; AUTO_DECIDE depends on it.

Completeness: use `Completeness: N/10` only when options differ in coverage. 10 = complete, 7 = happy path, 3 = shortcut. If options differ in kind, write: `Note: options differ in kind, not coverage — no completeness score.`

Pros / cons: use ✅ and ❌. Minimum 2 pros and 1 con per option when the choice is real; Minimum 40 characters per bullet. Hard-stop escape for one-way/destructive confirmations: `✅ No cons — this is a hard-stop choice`.

Neutral posture: `Recommendation: <default> — this is a taste call, no strong preference either way`; `(recommended)` STAYS on the default option for AUTO_DECIDE.

Effort both-scales: when an option involves effort, label both human-team and CC+gstack time, e.g. `(human: ~2 days / CC: ~15 min)`. Makes AI compression visible at decision time.

Net line closes the tradeoff. Per-skill instructions may add stricter rules.

### Handling 5+ options — split, never drop

AskUserQuestion caps every call at **4 options**. With 5+ real options, NEVER
drop, merge, or silently defer one to fit. Pick a compliant shape:

- **Batch into ≤4-groups** — for coherent alternatives (e.g. version bumps,
  layout variants). One call, 5th surfaced only if first 4 don't fit.
- **Split per-option** — for independent scope items (e.g. "ship E1..E6?").
  Fire N sequential calls, one per option. Default to this when unsure.

Per-option call shape: `D<N>.k` header (e.g. D3.1..D3.5), ELI10 per option,
Recommendation, kind-note (no completeness score — Include/Defer/Cut/Hold are
decision actions), and 4 buckets:
**A) Include**, **B) Defer**, **C) Cut**, **D) Hold** (stop chain, discuss).

After the chain, fire `D<N>.final` to validate the assembled set (reprompt
dependency conflicts) and confirm shipping it. Use `D<N>.revise-<k>` to
revise one option without re-running the chain.

For N>6, fire a `D<N>.0` meta-AskUserQuestion first (proceed / narrow / batch).

question_ids for split chains: `<skill>-split-<option-slug>` (kebab-case ASCII,
≤64 chars, `-2`/`-3` suffix on collision). The runtime checker
(`bin/gstack-question-preference`) refuses `never-ask` on any `*-split-*` id,
so split chains are never AUTO_DECIDE-eligible — the user's option set is sacred.

**Full rule + worked examples + Hold/dependency semantics:** see
`docs/askuserquestion-split.md` in the gstack repo. Read on demand when N>4.

**Non-ASCII characters — write directly, never \u-escape.** When any string
field contains Chinese (繁體/簡體), Japanese, Korean, or other non-ASCII text,
emit the literal UTF-8 characters; never escape them as `\uXXXX` (the pipe is
UTF-8 native, and manual escaping miscodes long CJK strings). Only `\n`,
`\t`, `\"`, `\\` remain allowed. Full rationale + worked example: see
`docs/askuserquestion-cjk.md`. Read on demand when a question contains CJK.

### Self-check before emitting

Before calling AskUserQuestion, verify:
- [ ] D<N> header present
- [ ] ELI10 paragraph present (stakes line too)
- [ ] Recommendation line present with concrete reason
- [ ] Completeness scored (coverage) OR kind-note present (kind)
- [ ] Every option has ≥2 ✅ and ≥1 ❌, each ≥40 chars (or hard-stop escape)
- [ ] (recommended) label on one option (even for neutral-posture)
- [ ] Dual-scale effort labels on effort-bearing options (human / CC)
- [ ] Net line closes the decision
- [ ] You are calling the tool, not writing prose — unless `CONDUCTOR_SESSION: true` (then prose is the DEFAULT, not the tool) OR the documented failure fallback applies (then: prose with the mandatory triad — issue ELI10, per-choice Completeness, Recommendation + `(recommended)` — and a "reply with a letter" instruction, then STOP)
- [ ] Non-ASCII characters (CJK / accents) written directly, NOT \u-escaped
- [ ] If you had 5+ options, you split (or batched into ≤4-groups) — did NOT drop any
- [ ] If you split, you checked dependencies between options before firing the chain
- [ ] If a per-option Hold fires, you stopped the chain immediately (didn't queue)


## Artifacts Sync (skill start)

```bash
_GSTACK_HOME="${GSTACK_HOME:-$HOME/.gstack}"
# Prefer the v1.27.0.0 artifacts file; fall back to brain file for users
# upgrading mid-stream before the migration script runs.
if [ -f "$HOME/.gstack-artifacts-remote.txt" ]; then
  _BRAIN_REMOTE_FILE="$HOME/.gstack-artifacts-remote.txt"
else
  _BRAIN_REMOTE_FILE="$HOME/.gstack-brain-remote.txt"
fi
_BRAIN_SYNC_BIN="~/.claude/skills/gstack/bin/gstack-brain-sync"
_BRAIN_CONFIG_BIN="~/.claude/skills/gstack/bin/gstack-config"

# /sync-gbrain context-load: teach the agent to use gbrain when it's available.
# Per-worktree pin: post-spike redesign uses kubectl-style `.gbrain-source` in the
# git toplevel to scope queries. Look for the pin in the worktree (not a global
# state file) so that opening worktree B without a pin doesn't claim "indexed"
# just because worktree A was synced. Empty string when gbrain is not
# configured (zero context cost for non-gbrain users).
_GBRAIN_CONFIG="$HOME/.gbrain/config.json"
if [ -f "$_GBRAIN_CONFIG" ] && command -v gbrain >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  _GBRAIN_VERSION_OK=$(gbrain --version 2>/dev/null | grep -c '^gbrain ' || echo 0)
  if [ "$_GBRAIN_VERSION_OK" -gt 0 ] 2>/dev/null; then
    _GBRAIN_PIN_PATH=""
    _REPO_TOP=$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel 2>/dev/null || echo "")
    if [ -n "$_REPO_TOP" ] && [ -f "$_REPO_TOP/.gbrain-source" ]; then
      _GBRAIN_PIN_PATH="$_REPO_TOP/.gbrain-source"
    fi
    if [ -n "$_GBRAIN_PIN_PATH" ]; then
      echo "GBrain configured. Prefer \`gbrain search\`/\`gbrain query\` over Grep for"
      echo "semantic questions; use \`gbrain code-def\`/\`code-refs\`/\`code-callers\` for"
      echo "symbol-aware code lookup. See \"## GBrain Search Guidance\" in CLAUDE.md."
      echo "Run /sync-gbrain to refresh."
    else
      echo "GBrain configured but this worktree isn't pinned yet. Run \`/sync-gbrain --full\`"
      echo "before relying on \`gbrain search\` for code questions in this worktree."
      echo "Falls back to Grep until pinned."
    fi
  fi
fi

_BRAIN_SYNC_MODE=$("$_BRAIN_CONFIG_BIN" get artifacts_sync_mode 2>/dev/null || echo off)

# Detect remote-MCP mode (Path 4 of /setup-gbrain). Local artifacts sync is
# a no-op in remote mode; the brain server pulls from GitHub/GitLab on its
# own cadence. Read claude.json directly to keep this preamble fast (no
# subprocess to claude CLI on every skill start).
_GBRAIN_MCP_MODE="none"
if command -v jq >/dev/null 2>&1 && [ -f "$HOME/.claude.json" ]; then
  _GBRAIN_MCP_TYPE=$(jq -r '.mcpServers.gbrain.type // .mcpServers.gbrain.transport // empty' "$HOME/.claude.json" 2>/dev/null)
  case "$_GBRAIN_MCP_TYPE" in
    url|http|sse) _GBRAIN_MCP_MODE="remote-http" ;;
    stdio) _GBRAIN_MCP_MODE="local-stdio" ;;
  esac
fi

if [ -f "$_BRAIN_REMOTE_FILE" ] && [ ! -d "$_GSTACK_HOME/.git" ] && [ "$_BRAIN_SYNC_MODE" = "off" ]; then
  _BRAIN_NEW_URL=$(head -1 "$_BRAIN_REMOTE_FILE" 2>/dev/null | tr -d '[:space:]')
  if [ -n "$_BRAIN_NEW_URL" ]; then
    echo "ARTIFACTS_SYNC: artifacts repo detected: $_BRAIN_NEW_URL"
    echo "ARTIFACTS_SYNC: run 'gstack-brain-restore' to pull your cross-machine artifacts (or 'gstack-config set artifacts_sync_mode off' to dismiss forever)"
  fi
fi

if [ -d "$_GSTACK_HOME/.git" ] && [ "$_BRAIN_SYNC_MODE" != "off" ]; then
  _BRAIN_LAST_PULL_FILE="$_GSTACK_HOME/.brain-last-pull"
  _BRAIN_NOW=$(date +%s)
  _BRAIN_DO_PULL=1
  if [ -f "$_BRAIN_LAST_PULL_FILE" ]; then
    _BRAIN_LAST=$(cat "$_BRAIN_LAST_PULL_FILE" 2>/dev/null || echo 0)
    _BRAIN_AGE=$(( _BRAIN_NOW - _BRAIN_LAST ))
    [ "$_BRAIN_AGE" -lt 86400 ] && _BRAIN_DO_PULL=0
  fi
  if [ "$_BRAIN_DO_PULL" = "1" ]; then
    ( cd "$_GSTACK_HOME" && git fetch origin >/dev/null 2>&1 && git merge --ff-only "origin/$(git rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD)" >/dev/null 2>&1 ) || true
    echo "$_BRAIN_NOW" > "$_BRAIN_LAST_PULL_FILE"
  fi
  "$_BRAIN_SYNC_BIN" --once 2>/dev/null || true
fi

if [ "$_GBRAIN_MCP_MODE" = "remote-http" ]; then
  # Remote-MCP mode: local artifacts sync is a no-op (brain admin's server
  # pulls from GitHub/GitLab). Show the user this is by design, not broken.
  _GBRAIN_HOST=$(jq -r '.mcpServers.gbrain.url // empty' "$HOME/.claude.json" 2>/dev/null | sed -E 's|^https?://([^/:]+).*|\1|')
  echo "ARTIFACTS_SYNC: remote-mode (managed by brain server ${_GBRAIN_HOST:-remote})"
elif [ -d "$_GSTACK_HOME/.git" ] && [ "$_BRAIN_SYNC_MODE" != "off" ]; then
  _BRAIN_QUEUE_DEPTH=0
  [ -f "$_GSTACK_HOME/.brain-queue.jsonl" ] && _BRAIN_QUEUE_DEPTH=$(wc -l < "$_GSTACK_HOME/.brain-queue.jsonl" | tr -d ' ')
  _BRAIN_LAST_PUSH="never"
  [ -f "$_GSTACK_HOME/.brain-last-push" ] && _BRAIN_LAST_PUSH=$(cat "$_GSTACK_HOME/.brain-last-push" 2>/dev/null || echo never)
  echo "ARTIFACTS_SYNC: mode=$_BRAIN_SYNC_MODE | last_push=$_BRAIN_LAST_PUSH | queue=$_BRAIN_QUEUE_DEPTH"
else
  echo "ARTIFACTS_SYNC: off"
fi
```
